The open question is what happens to B's list scroll position when the user goes back to a previous page.                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm weighing how to keep prefetch from running ahead of what the user actually needs, since lazy-loading feeds would trigger real network loads on B if the capture head scrolls too far. I'm leaning toward capping the     
 lookahead by time, with lead distance set from the measured velocity and a tail latency plus margin, rather than scrolling until the bottom.                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm noting that the scrollbar can be estimated for RecyclerView from the item count and the average item pitch, since the content height isn't directly exposed.                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how scrollbar pixels fit the 0px contract: I'd detect the thin right-edge strip after compensating for scroll, drop it from both transmission and the map, and exclude it from the pixel-equality guarantee,     
 since A draws its own scrollbar from the region data.                                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working through the scrollbar issue: the thin scrollbar strip can be excluded from hashing and transmission, since A draws its own. The pixels under the thumb still have to be recorded once the thumb fades, so the map     
 stays complete.                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling how the scrollbar band should fill in the map: columns under the thumb get a provisional value from the left neighbor and are only finalized once the thumb fades after settling. I'm also wondering whether         
 animations disabled would make ripples instant, and how that would change the :active overlay timing.                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm proposing that B keep a shadow map of committed content, so a change shows up as an immediate overlay for feedback and only gets committed once it stays stable past a threshold. If the content reverts to the committed     
 hash, the overlay just ends, and a permanent change can be promoted from overlay to tile with a small commit op instead of resending the pixels.                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling the back-stack behavior: A keeps a stack of page maps, so Back shows the cached page instantly while B verifies and sends any diffs. Tapping forward can work the same way, showing a cached child page right    
 away while B loads the live one.                                                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on a per-column-band hash, splitting each row into 4–8 bands, so a change can be localized horizontally and the dirty region stays 2D. Shown as a stale-while-revalidate option, cached pages appear instantly with  
 a faint "unverified" marker until B confirms the page hash, keyed by the tapped node's identity.                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now working through how to hash each row in column segments, perhaps 64 or 128 pixels wide, so the full-row hash is just a fold of those. That keeps the cost the same while allowing localized dirty rectangles and making   
 it easier to spot horizontal shifts later.                                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now weighing a per-row information weight: counting horizontal color transitions gives a cheap signal, and discounting rows whose hash repeats within the frame handles periodic lists and blank dividers.

 Now I'm considering how collapsing toolbars could break the model, since the header shrinks while the list scrolls and its region doesn't move rigidly. I'm thinking of treating the collapse range as a separate header zone

 I'm working through the collapsing header: the top part of the screen doesn't move rigidly while the list scrolls, so I'd cache both the expanded and collapsed variants and switch between them at the threshold rather than     
 chasing exact pixels during the transition. I can spot this zone in the frames because those rows don't match either a zero shift or the list's shift.                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now looking at how fixed header elements change with scroll state, since a top app bar may shift color once content scrolls under it, so A would need both an at-top and a scrolled variant of the header.                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm noting that overscroll stretch doesn't need to go through the protocol, since B clamps its scroll at the top and bottom and never produces stretch frames. If a stretch does show up from an overshooting drag, I'd spot it

 I'm considering what happens when the list's item heights vary, since content coordinates still accumulate from the pixel-vote dy rather than from item indices. The harder cases are when heights shift after images load, when  
 rows get inserted, or when a jump scroll leaves no pixel overlap, which would open an island in the map with an unknown offset.                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing the idea of representing the map as a set of anchored segments that merge when hashes overlap, rather than one continuous axis, since a jump scroll would otherwise break it. A11y row indices could give the rough

 I'm considering how the map handles jump scrolls: a fast-scroller or accessibility jump can leave no pixel overlap, so the map would need separate segments that merge once they match. I'm also weighing a handshake where each

 I'm weighing a content-addressed store on A, with chunks keyed by hash and a page map that B diffs against what A reports missing as a bitmap. That makes the cache revisions just a fast path rather than something correctness  
 depends on, and it means A can evict chunks freely without breaking the sync.  Now I'm looking at chunk boundaries: a fixed 64-row grid would shift whenever the content origin differs on re-entry, so I'd cut at blank divider rows between items instead, which keeps hashes stable under shifts and

 I'm settling on how to cut the content into chunks: rather than a fixed row grid that would shift whenever the origin differs, I'd cut at the low-information valleys between items, capped at about 256 rows, with the A11y item 
 bounds as a prior.  Now I'm noting the pitfalls with the scroll approach: Android 12+ stretch overscroll isn't rigid, so horizontal offsets need their own layout protocol entry, and a re-entered page may come back at a different scroll position. 
 Rounded icon edges blend with the background, and dialog dimming, column shifts, and spinner motion can all invalidate tiles.

 I'm moving on to the scroll model, where A's viewport and B's capture origin are separate coordinates, and a tap at a page position has to land inside B's current capture window before it maps to B's screen y.

 I'm estimating how fast the content can actually be supplied: at roughly 300 KB/s, a text-heavy screen of around 70–150 KB works out to about 2–4 screens per second, and image-heavy pages to around 1.5–3. Next I need to check

 I'm working out how fast the scroll can be driven: injected wheel events could move the app far faster than the network delivers content, so the real limit is bandwidth. Prefetch needs to be scheduled against the bandwidth

 I'm settling on the fling: since the viewer computes where the scroll will land, A can send that target ahead of time, letting B jump the capture head there and prefetch the landing area first, then backfill the content the

 I'm settling on deadline scheduling for the tiles: each one is ordered by when A's viewport will reach it compared with how long it takes to deliver, and anything that can't arrive in time gets pushed to the idle backfill     
 queue. For continuous drag or wheel scrolling, where the landing spot isn't known, I'll stick with the lead formula of speed times P95 plus margin. On the B side, I'm now checking how the app can be scrolled from its current

 I'm working out how a scrollbar drag would map to a content position, using the accessibility scroll extent and the item count to estimate the total content height. That estimate only holds when item heights are uniform, so

 I'm working out how the scrollbar's fade can be handled: the thumb pollutes the right-edge columns during scrolling and for a while after, so the plan is to treat those pixels as provisional and confirm them in a later pass

 I'm thinking through how transient changes like ripples, spinners, cursor blinks, and clocks should be kept out of the base image. The idea is to classify each changed region by how its content behaves over time: if it        
 returns to the base appearance within a short window after a touch, it counts as transient and goes into an overlay rather than the base. The overlay gets sent right away without waiting, so nothing is delayed in display.     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on the commit rule for the overlay: a region gets promoted to the base map once it has stayed stable for a few hundred milliseconds with no touch down, and it gets cleared if its pixels return to the base hash.   
 That means the protocol only needs Patch with a volatile flag followed by either Commit or Revert, so no pixels are resent on commit.

 I'm weighing the lossy codec for the image interiors now: JPEG looks like the best fit, since Android's own Bitmap.compress already uses a hardware-tuned libjpeg-turbo, so I wouldn't need extra dependencies. Encoding through

 I'm working out the prefetch scheduling model, starting with how to measure drawing latency without syncing clocks: the sender timestamps each tile when it's scheduled, and the receiver's ack carries its draw time, so the     
 round-trip delta minus half the RTT gives a usable per-app estimate. Next I'm defining the viewport position and velocity on the receiver, the map's covered intervals, and the sender's capture window that those drive.         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out the prefetch scheduling: the predicted sweep covers the viewport plus one tall region ahead in the scroll direction, minus what's already mapped. B then positions its capture window to cover that span and      
 encodes the missing bands in order of when they'll be needed, sending them only when the visible queue is empty. When the display is idle, it keeps extending coverage in the last scroll direction up to a per-app budget of a

 I'm settling the invariant for prefetch: the capture window always has to contain A's current viewport, so any tap lands on content that's already on B's screen without a pre-scroll. Prefetch can then only reach about one     
 extra region away from the viewport, and beyond that the capture head moves forward only while the display is idle.                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the trade-off for prefetch on the tall display: the default is that the capture window always contains the viewport, so taps never need a scroll first, and roaming ahead is only an optional per-app excursion.     
 Non-tall pages can't keep that invariant, since fetching ahead means the capture head has to leave the viewport, so I'm treating them separately.                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the default for non-eligible pages: no prefetch, with the capture head simply following the viewport on demand. Roaming ahead would stay an optional extension, and the tall-display method is what the idea

 I'm settling on a two-level layout: a content-addressed strip store keyed by hash for deduplication and persistence, and a page map of content-y offsets pointing into those strips. The coordinate index is there for latency    
 and decoupling, since the viewer needs to know where content lands without waiting on the server, rather than for saving bytes.                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm thinking about how the page map could be built from content-addressed strips, like a git tree over blobs: each page is an ordered list of strip hashes, so comparing page revisions reduces to comparing those lists. The 
 open question is how to cut strips so that identical content still produces identical hashes at different scroll offsets, which points toward content-defined chunking rather than fixed screen positions.                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm pinning down how strips get cut: at content-defined boundaries, using the blank rows between list items, so each item usually becomes its own strip. That keeps hashes stable across scroll positions, and an inserted    
 item only shifts later coordinates without invalidating them, which improves on GOAL 3.2's invalidate-and-fall-back approach.                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how the strips get cut when there are no blank rows, like in photos or large text blocks. The fallback is to cap strip height at about 256 rows and fall back to fixed offsets from the last boundary, or to  
 cut by the accessibility bounds for photo regions. Small strips, around 16 rows minimum, get merged, and that overhead stays low. The awkward case is an item only half-visible at the bottom edge, since its hash isn't known    
 until it's fully on screen, so I'm considering sending those partial rows as provisional literal rows in the map.                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing fixed-height tiles in content coordinates against the content-defined strips, since tiles are simpler but shift on insertions. A copy operation with an arbitrary source offset from the map could absorb that       
 misalignment without resending everything.                                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a row-level hash index against content-addressed strips. Coordinate tiles with a global row-hash index would get the same deduplication through Copy operations, and at roughly 8 MB for a million rows it's         
 affordable. It's the more straightforward design because rows themselves are the unit.                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a row-level design against the content-addressed strips: keeping rows as the atomic unit, stored as intervals, avoids fixed tile sizes and content-defined chunking. On revisit, I'd recompute row hashes for the    
 captured frame, locate the first screen by voting against the stored row-hash array, and send only the mismatched row runs. Insertions would need the same voting to realign.                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how to align the two sequences of row hashes, since the same primitive could handle scroll detection, map relocation, and revisit diffs. The idea is to compare a reference sequence against the current one  
 and get back matched runs with their offsets, weighted by how much information each run carries. Insertions would then show up as shifted matches, so only the inserted rows need to be sent as literals.                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on one primitive, a weighted alignment of row-hash sequences, to handle scroll detection, map relocation, revisit diffs, and cross-page reuse. That's simpler than the separate mechanisms GOAL lists, and I'd       
 rather keep that than add content-defined strips on top.                                                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on Hello handshakes scoped to the session's app, since hundreds of pages would be wasteful to advertise all at once. Then I'm turning to how B learns what A has dropped: silent eviction would desync the belief,   
 so I'm weighing whether to report evictions explicitly.                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at how to handle the accessibility side: tree dumps are slow, so I'd rely on incremental events like content-changed and view-scrolled, and I'd also plan to check a rolling hash of the visible rows as a        
 debug-mode verification.                                                                                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm covering how the user taps on A's display get routed back to B: I'll express taps in page content coordinates (region plus content position), have B translate them into its own capture-head screen coordinates, and    
 scroll first if the target is outside the current window. Since the user may tap a view that A has already moved past, each tap should carry the page revision A was showing, so B can reject taps on stale content.              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at how tap input gets routed back: a tap on the stale view is rejected if the row hashes inside the tapped node's bounds have changed since A's seen revision. For keyboard input, I'm thinking about how the IME 
 should behave on the virtual display, with key events for ASCII and clipboard paste for non-ASCII text.                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing whether to keep an explicit eviction report from A to B, or to handle misses lazily, and I'm settling on the screen-coordinate hide policy as a first-milestone item so the IME stays off both the virtual       
 display and B's physical screen.                                                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the certificate setup, since the WebTransport serverCertificateHashes option only accepts certificates valid for under two weeks.                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the WebTransport certificate option next, since serverCertificateHashes only works with certificates valid for under two weeks. The IDEA notes suggest the cert hash in the WebUI URL could serve as the auth token, 
 though the hash is fairly public, so I'm questioning whether that's enough protection.                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing whether the cert hash in the URL can serve as authentication at all, since the server cert is sent in the clear to anyone who connects, which makes the hash effectively public. I'm considering a separate      
 random token in the URL instead, since it would cost almost nothing to add.                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm looking at how the certificate hash in the URL holds up as authentication, since the server cert is sent in the clear and its hash is effectively public. I'm also thinking about cert rotation: the daemon would regenerate  
 the cert within the two-week limit and print a new URL, so a stale URL just means re-pairing, and I still need to figure out what serves the localhost WebUI on A.                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Checking the MTU math now: Tailscale's 1280 leaves enough room for QUIC's 1200-byte minimum over both IPv4 and IPv6, so the datagram payload limit works out.                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the datagram size limit now: with the Tailscale MTU of 1280, QUIC's 1200-byte minimum fits, leaving roughly 1150 to 1200 bytes after headers, so I'll keep application payloads under about 1100 bytes. To avoid     
 black-holed probes, I'm leaning toward turning off path MTU discovery and pinning the initial MTU at 1200.                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm deciding what goes over the datagram channel: scroll positions, sent as absolute targets so each newer one supersedes the last, while taps, keys, and back presses stay on the reliable stream.                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing how to keep the uplink from bloating queues: I'd run an app-level token bucket at roughly 85% of the estimated bandwidth, using QUIC's stats for the budget. When traffic falls back through DERP relays, which  
 run over TCP, I'd assume a more conservative rate since the buffering there is worse.                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing a tile-based viewer where the scroll region is a real scrollable container holding canvas tiles, so the browser handles momentum, wheel, and scrollbar natively with no per-frame JavaScript.                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm thinking about the page-space mapping: the scroll offset the browser reports, at device-pixel scale, maps one-to-one onto content coordinates, so I'd convert through the devicePixelRatio before sending a ScrollTo to   
 B.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing a DOM-native scroll container with tile canvases against a custom rAF compositor: the browser's own scroll physics would handle momentum and the scrollbar, and I'd only need to map the scroll offset through   
 devicePixelRatio to content coordinates, accepting that fractional offsets blur slightly during motion.                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether the viewer should be a native DOM scroll container holding tile canvases, since that would give browser momentum and scrollbars for free, and I still need to decide whether that's worth the pitfalls I'd   
 have to check.                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm laying out the offline groundwork: a recorder on the host that captures frames, accessibility data, and timestamped input, plus a replay harness with a link simulator to measure bytes, peak rates, and latency against  
 a scrcpy baseline. I'm also setting up a feature-flag table so each ablation can be toggled from one place.                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm deciding on the output format for the plan: either rewriting GOAL.md in place or writing a separate document, and I'm leaning toward a separate plan file so the outdated GOAL.md stays untouched.                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm deciding whether to rewrite GOAL.md in place with the improved plan or just answer in chat. Since GOAL.md is stale and the file is under git, updating it seems safe, and IDEA.md stays untouched as the authority.           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm checking the Android API details I plan to cite, starting with the UiAutomation flags, so the plan doesn't claim anything I haven't verified.                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Checking the Android UiAutomation and accessibility event APIs I plan to cite, so the plan doesn't claim anything unverified.                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how RecyclerView reports scroll in accessibility events, since I'm not sure it fills in scrollY and maxScrollY reliably, and I'm wondering whether the scroll deltas are the more dependable signal.             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how RecyclerView reports scroll to accessibility, since its events carry accumulated deltas rather than absolute offsets, and I'm weighing whether the item row indices from the collection info are a more      
 dependable position signal.                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how RecyclerView fills in accessibility collection info for items, since the row index guess depends on whether the layout manager scrolls vertically.                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how RecyclerView exposes item positions to accessibility: the row index and total count on each item could give an absolute offset without drift, which would address the concern that RecyclerView has no       
 absolute scroll offset.                                                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out that the A11y event's scroll deltas are accumulated and can drift, but RecyclerView's item row index and total count could anchor the map by item position instead.                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how accessibility scroll events behave on Compose and ScrollView. Scroll events might report absolute offsets for ScrollView, but Compose's LazyColumn is less clear, so I'll mark that coverage as something to 
 measure in M0b.                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at whether the absolute scroll offset can come straight from the accessibility data: ScrollView reports scrollY against maxScrollY, and RecyclerView's item row index against the total count could give an       
 approximate position. I'm also considering ACTION_SCROLL_TO_POSITION, which would let B jump the capture head directly to an item index.                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking whether RecyclerView's accessibility scroll action can jump straight to an item index, since I think the layout manager handles ACTION_SCROLL_TO_POSITION, though I'm not certain which recyclerview versions    
 support it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the remaining API claims: VirtualDisplay.resize is available from API 21, and the WebCodecs path for the foreground looks plausible. The quinn and wtransport priority setting is confirmed, though the send     
 order only applies to streams the client creates.                                                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the bandwidth numbers: at 300KB/s, a 100ms window allows about 30KB, and the old steady-state frames at 4–11KB fit that budget, though page-change frames need a closer look.                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm comparing the old WebP lossless numbers against the link budget: at 300KB/s, saving about 80KB is roughly 267ms on the wire, which is more than the 196ms it takes to encode a full text screen, so the earlier "not      
 real-time" verdict may not hold on this link.                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out the encode-versus-transmit tradeoff: at about 300KB/s, each millisecond of encoding is worth roughly 300 bytes of saved traffic, so a slower encoder can still win. I'm also considering streaming strips top 
 to bottom so encoding overlaps with sending, as long as the encoder keeps up with the link rate.                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working through the bandwidth tradeoff: at about 300 KB/s, a slower encoder can still come out ahead, since saving 23 KB on a 150 KB frame is worth roughly 78 ms of link time. I'm thinking the palette-mode codec       
 should get close to WebP-lossless size on text, with strips pipelined so encoding overlaps transmission.                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Parallelizing the encode across strips is a cheap lever the old design never used, since its measurements were single-threaded. The phone has around eight cores, so a text screen that took about 196ms on one core could drop   
 to roughly 25–40ms split across a thread pool. That makes a WebP-lossless-style encode viable without writing a custom codec first.                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm weighing whether to use libwebp lossless as a reference encoder in the offline bench, since IDEA.md's own codec plan still leads, and checking whether our Palette+IBC approach can beat its byte count at a reasonable  
 encode cost.                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Now I'm thinking about how the IDEA doc frames the virtual display: it wants a very tall virtual screen so the scroll region can be prefetched in bulk, rather than syncing narrow pixel strips as each scroll frame reveals      
 them. The scrollbar and how far ahead to prefetch both need care, measured in latency.                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how the tall virtual display would hold up against texture limits: the plan says to keep it at roughly three to four times the screen height, and a 1080×10560 surface could run past the maximum texture or     
 layer size on some GPUs and compositor paths.                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the virtual display size limits: the plan keeps it at roughly three to four times the screen height, and at the 1080×2400 resolution I'm mindful that tall surfaces can exceed GPU texture limits, so the spike  
 needs to find the largest height each device handles.                                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how the tall virtual display would be judged eligible: I'd look at the accessibility tree for a scroll region that spans the full width and runs down to the bottom of the screen, and for a bottom bar sitting  
 at the base. Pixels could confirm it too, but resizing the display to compare is too costly, so the tree is the main signal, with a floating button in the bottom-right needing separate handling.                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how to make the tall virtual display handle the fixed bottom-right button: the button is an opaque core with a semi-transparent shadow, so where it sits over scrolling content its pixels blend with what's  
 behind, and they can't be cleanly separated from the content.                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing how the tall virtual display would be judged eligible: either the page falls outside the tall-display rule, or the floating button's semi-transparent shadow gets recovered by capturing it over two known           
 backgrounds and solving for alpha per pixel.                                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether a fixed overlay like the floating button should make a page ineligible for the tall virtual display on the first pass, and falling back to prefetching the head of the page instead. Even without the tall   
 display, any overlay sitting over scrolling content runs into the same alpha problem, so I'm considering whether to leave that for a later matting step.                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling how the decoupled viewers behave at rest: the 0px promise only has to hold once scrolling stops, so the overlay halo can be approximate mid-motion and should snap to exact once B converges to A's offset.      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the FAB case: if a fixed overlay sits inside the scroll rectangle, the page can't use the tall display and falls back to an equal-height virtual display, since only then can the offsets match exactly at rest.     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing the capture-head prefetch as the fallback for FAB pages without a tall display: while the user is idle, B scrolls ahead to capture more content, then returns to the current position so taps respond instantly  
 and the rest state stays exact. A tap that lands during that excursion would have to wait for B to scroll back first.                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how to spot the scrollbar: it can't be turned off globally and fades in and out during scrolling, so I'm thinking of detecting its narrow right-edge column from the residual left after compensating for the 
 scroll shift, then masking it out of the hashes and leaving it for the viewer to draw.                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm handling the scrollbar: its column band has to be found from the residual left after compensating for the scroll shift, and I can't count on the accessibility tree to report it. Once it's located, I'll drop that       
 column from the hashes and commit pixels there only when they match the rigid-shift prediction, or once the scrollbar has faded after scrolling stops.                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm moving on to animations: the plan is to turn off window and transition animations and blur, and to make the animator duration adjustable, since a scale of zero makes ripples and progress animations jump straight to    
 their end state. Some apps misbehave at zero, though, so that needs checking. The original settings get saved to /data/local/tmp so they can be restored even after a hard kill.                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm handling session and back navigation: ESC or right-click maps to Back, and the browser history gets pushState so its back button matches. At the root, the session ends instead of sending Back, and the back stack's    
 IBC gets recorded.                                                                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling how the back stack feeds the design: on Back the page can be shown instantly from cache and then checked against the live screen, and on Esc the app already knows the parent page, so it can show that right away.  
 I'll detect page changes from accessibility window-state events and skeleton hashes rather than the old slow dumpsys polling, and track the stack on the B side.                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm treating a Back press as an expected response: after injecting it, the stack should pop, and after a tap it should push or stay put, so the recognizer checks that prediction before searching blindly. Page skeletons   
 also shift while content loads, so I'll only compute a PageId once the frame has held steady and the accessibility tree has gone quiet.                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm settling how to split the page-skeleton fingerprint from the list content: I'll strip the list items and hash only the resource-id structure, then add title text as an extra discriminator where the skeletons collide, 
 since Settings subpages look alike by resource-id alone.                                                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing the density-dependent tile size next: the block size for classification should scale with DPI, so I'm looking at whether rounding to a multiple of 4 px holds up on high-density screens.                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working through the per-app palette prior now: a global palette of the most frequent colors per app can be preloaded as base indices, so each block's palette can reference those entries instead of sending its own, and a   
 theme switch would select a different palette set.                                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing the on-screen stats panel: it should show savings for the sprite cache, scrolling, and long-screenshot page map, and the exact shadow-encoding comparison is too costly to run all the time, so I'll estimate    
 the literal bytes online from area times the running average per class and save exact shadow encoding for offline benchmarks. I'm also planning one tunables registry holding key, default, range, step, group, and per-app       
 override, which the panel and encoder both read.                                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at the per-app profile: scrollbar width, prefetch mode, lead margin, static policy, palette base, and similar settings get stored per package on the B side, with shipped defaults taken from the corpus.         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm sketching the wire protocol changes: tile messages become row-based regions with an explicit height, x-origin, and optional width, and copy ops unify sources from the page map, a sprite, or the previous screen.        
 Regions also pick up axis, anchor, scrollbar width, pitch, row count, and an exact flag, while pages gain discriminators and a policy field.                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm sketching the wire-level layout: a view-report message replacing the old scroll command, since A only says where its viewport sits and how fast it's moving, and B decides where the capture head goes. Taps carry the    
 page and revision they were made against, and the streams split into a reliable control channel, a high-priority visible stream, cancellable prefetch chunks, and resettable per-frame streams.                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm thinking about the A-side memory budget: the old build used around 140MB of WASM memory, split between a 96MB pool and a 32MB map. For the new design I'm considering persisting the received encoded form in OPFS with

 Now I'm settling how the decoded pages get stored: the A side persists them in OPFS with an LRU keyed by page, and it re-encodes each page into a self-contained form during idle time, since the streamed form depends on zstd   
 context and IBC references that won't survive on their own.                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out the signal-processing table for recognizing page changes, starting with displacement. The method tries a row-signature sequence first, checks the predicted shift within a window, and falls back to a        
 weighted histogram vote if that fails.                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm laying out the signal-processing table for recognizing displacement and page changes: the row-signature and normalized cross-correlation fallback each have a cost if they go wrong, mostly extra literal bytes sent. Next    
 I'm working through how the scrollbar column and the item pitch get picked up from the residual and the row-summary autocorrelation.                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now laying out the signal-processing table for the remaining recognizers: the block classifier decides between text, image, and flat regions from color count, run counts, and gradient share, and I'm weighing the cost when 
 it picks the wrong mode. Next I'm looking at how connected components get grouped into text bounding boxes, and how the transient-state tracker should debounce each rectangle's hash over time.                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Still laying out the signal-processing table: for each recognizer I'm weighing the signal, the method, the prior it uses, and what it costs when it gets the answer wrong. I'm working through displacement, scroll-bar           
 detection, and the block classifier, and the next rows cover dimming and page switches.                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing the window-event signal for page changes: a coverage threshold plus a skeleton hash, checked right after a Tap or Back is injected, since a wrong call only costs one extra relocation. I'm also adding a        
 rate-distortion step where the classifier only proposes one or two modes per block, and the actual trial-encoded byte count picks the winner when the budget allows.                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing the page-cache priority against scroll: the old numbers showed the back-cache was worth far more than scroll COPY, so the bytes to cut are on first appearance and page switches. I'm planning to move the       
 map-and-alignment primitive up to M2, since scroll-back and page-back both reduce to aligning the current frame against a stored map, with the viewer's local scroll and prefetch after that.

 I'm comparing the old numbers against the new design, noting that the page cache mattered far more than scroll for bytes, and that local composition on A is the only way to beat the app's own render latency.

 I've got what I need, so now I'm working out what the deliverable should be. The request is to improve the plan, with no testing. IDEA.md is the reference standard, GOAL.md is outdated, and the user plans to rewrite it, so    
 I'm considering whether I should rewrite GOAL.md.                                                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm deciding the deliverable now: the user wants the plan improved and IDEA.md is the reference to leave untouched. GOAL.md is stale, and since it's tracked in git, updating it in place is safe to do, so I'll rewrite it and   
 report the changes.                                                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the technical claims I plan to make. The WebTransport certificate hash rules look confirmed, but GOAL.md's use of sendOrder is wrong for server-to-client data, so the server has to set stream priority itself. I   
 also need to account for the fact that data already handed to the QUIC send buffer can't be reordered, so prefetch writes should go out in small chunks.                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the QUIC packet-size math next: over a Tailscale tunnel with a 1280 MTU, the UDP payload drops to about 1252 bytes on IPv4 or 1232 on IPv6, which is close to QUIC's 1200-byte minimum. Quinn's MTU probing assumes  
 a larger ceiling, so oversized sends could fail locally with EMSGSIZE.                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Checking the MTU numbers against quinn's defaults: over a 1280-byte tunnel, the QUIC payload ceiling is about 1252 on IPv4 and 1232 on IPv6, so any probe above that would fail locally. Capping the upper bound at 1232, or      
 turning MTU discovery off and keeping the 1200 initial MTU, avoids that. I think the datagram budget should stay around 1100 bytes to leave room for headers, though I haven't confirmed quinn's default upper bound of 1452.     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm checking how UiAutomation is used from a shell process, since it needs the hidden constructor and a connection, the same way uiautomator does it. I also want to confirm quinn's default MTU upper bound, which I        
 haven't verified yet, before I state it as fact.                                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking how the accessibility events from RecyclerView expose scroll position, since LinearLayoutManager sets the first and last visible item indices on each event rather than an absolute offset.                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now checking how the accessibility node info for each list item exposes its row index, since the default LayoutManager sets that from the item's adapter position. That would let me anchor the map on (item index, offset    
 within the item) rather than relying on accumulated pixel deltas, which I think is more robust.                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm planning to check the RecyclerView source on GitHub, specifically onInitializeAccessibilityNodeInfoForItem and LinearLayoutManager's onInitializeAccessibilityEvent, since the anchor design depends on them. I'll flag these 
 as items to verify on device in M0 rather than treat them as confirmed, and I'm noting that the uiautomator XML in the corpus lacks collection info, scroll events, and window data, so the new recorder should read              
 AccessibilityNodeInfo fields directly.                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing how to move the capture head on B: performAction(ACTION_SCROLL_FORWARD) on a RecyclerView runs an animated smooth scroll by roughly a page, which is neither precise nor instant, so it's a poor fit for fixed-step  
 injection.                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing the remaining ways to move the capture head on B, since performAction with ACTION_SCROLL_TO_POSITION may or may not be honored by LinearLayoutManager in the androidx version in use, and I'd need to verify that.   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now looking into how RecyclerView handles mouse wheel input, since it may scroll by a precise delta in some androidx versions and with an animation in others, which would matter for fixed-step injection.                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the default scroll quantum for a mouse wheel notch, since AXIS_VSCROLL is a float and the per-notch distance determines how precise the fixed-step injection can be.                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a per-app probe for wheel-injected scrolling: at page entry, inject a known pixel amount and check whether the pixel vote shows an exact, animated, or unsupported response, then fall back accordingly, since       
 Compose's mouse wheel handling may animate depending on version.                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing the tall virtual display option next: the idea is to fix the display height once per app session from a saved config, rather than resizing per page. The IDEA doc ties it to pages that have a single scroll region  
 reaching the screen bottom or a 100vw bottom bar, so I'd make it default-on only for those pages.                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Resizing the virtual display per page would trigger a configuration change and possibly an Activity relaunch, which is an M0 risk. A fixed tall display set once per session avoids that, but a page that doesn't qualify would   
 then be laid out for a tall screen and the viewer couldn't show it correctly, so the per-page logic needs more thought.                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether resizing the virtual display per page is workable, since a config change could recreate the Activity and drop the scroll position. The alternatives are a tall display with task bounds set by am task       
 resize, which has the same config-change problem, or switching displays, which forces a relaunch. The real catch is that a page only qualifies after its accessibility tree is read, so the resize would land mid-session, right  
 after the page is already on screen.                                                                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm considering whether a tall display could stay on for the whole session, but pages that don't qualify would then be laid out for a taller screen and break the viewer, so per-page resizing still looks like the lesser risk.  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing the tall-display tradeoff again: a page that isn't a single scroll region would be laid out for a taller screen and break the viewer, so the plan needs to decide on a strategy. I'll have M0 measure the        
 candidate approaches and pick one, keeping the protocol in page-space coordinates. I also need to flag that with a tall screen, input coordinates and tap mapping change, which the plan doesn't address yet.                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now weighing the tall-screen side effects: a 3× display means roughly 31MB per frame, and the hashing cost scales about threefold, around 6.6ms per frame on the old phone measurement. Seven-thousand-plus pixel heights may 
 also exceed the texture limit on older GPUs, so I'll have the plan cap the multiplier and note that ImageReader delivers the full buffer every frame.
