 I'm noticing an asymmetry in the tall display: a scroll of dy exposes content far below the viewport, so the capture head stays about (k-1)·H ahead going down, but nothing is captured ahead going up. Upward content is usually 
 already in the map since lists start at the top, except after re-entry at a mid-list position, so idle-time prefetch could cover that gap.                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now thinking about how the capture head should be scheduled: the viewport position and the scroll target need to stay inside the map's coverage, with the target moving based on scroll direction. Then I'm turning to the    
 main gap in GOAL: it decouples the viewer's viewport from the real scroll position, but doesn't yet say how to keep the cached map correct when it goes stale.                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now looking at how the cached map stays valid when the viewer shows content B isn't currently displaying. IDEA accepts that default static assumption, so the plan needs a revalidation step: when B's capture window passes  
 over mapped content, it compares row hashes against what it stored and sends only the differences. GOAL's whole-page reset on a cache or page revision mismatch is the fallback I'm trying to improve on.                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how to make the page map reconcile per segment instead of resetting the whole page on a revision mismatch. Since B only keeps hashes, not pixels, it can't replay changed content, so it would mark the segments  
 written after A's last acknowledged revision as absent and resend them when they're next captured.                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm thinking about how a per-segment revision could replace the whole-page reset: B tracks which segments it wrote after A's last acknowledged revision and resends only those. If B has lost its state, A could send its hash    
 inventory on connect so B can rebuild without persisting anything itself, which would make A the source of truth.                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now checking whether a page's skeleton hash can tell pages apart, since many Settings sub-pages share the same host activity and RecyclerView structure. Once list item subtrees are removed, their skeletons look identical, 
 so the title text is probably what has to distinguish them.                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Page identity needs more than the skeleton hash, since many Settings sub-pages share the same host structure. I'm weighing whether the title text and Activity component can serve as the key, and whether a pixel-hash check on  
 the first screen catches wrong matches.                                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now looking at page identity for a different purpose: the client has to show a cached page instantly on Back, before B confirms it. That speculative frame is drawn from the map, and B's confirmation, carrying hashes, will 
 patch any segments that turn out to differ.                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on a page key built from the package, activity class, window title, and a skeleton hash of the non-scrolling chrome, since dynamic sections like loading spinners would shift a plain skeleton hash. The back stack  
 would hold that key plus a scroll anchor, and I'm looking at using the first visible item's adapter position and top offset from the accessibility collection info to relocate the viewport on re-entry.                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now checking the row-hash voting details in GOAL: the hash should cover only the scroll-region columns, with the right-edge scrollbar strip excluded, and I'm weighing whether a fixed dp width for that strip is good        
 enough.                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing the row-hash weighting next: instead of run counts alone, each row gets weighted by how rare its hash is among the previous frame's rows, so separators and solid-color padding barely count. I'm also planning to   
 use B's own injected scroll amount as the expected dy and verify that first, falling back to voting only when the check fails.                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now looking at how to verify displacement: since B does the scrolling itself, the expected offset is already known, so checking that hypothesis first replaces a broad search and voting is kept only for app-initiated       
 scrolls. I'm also noting that sticky headers and collapsing toolbars can produce several displacements, so I'll limit that to a few rounds within the scrollable rects, and that row hashes should be taken per column band       
 inside the scroll region rather than across whole rows.                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now weighing how the Palette mode for the IBC encoding should be laid out, since GOAL leaves the enum variant undefined, and I'm considering whether the block unit should be small horizontal strips of rows or 64×64        
 blocks, with a "copy above" mode for the repetitive text-like content.                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing palette-index coding for the Palette mode: mapping pixels to indices, then a row-above predictor, then zstd, which is how PNG-8 gets its gains. The old measurement shows WebP lossless beating plain RGB+zstd on    
 text pages, so I'm checking what palette and back-reference tricks account for that gap.                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing palette-index coding as a middle ground between raw RGB+zstd and WebP lossless, since antialiased text on a solid background lies along a single color line and can be indexed compactly. The plan is to benchmark a 
 few candidates offline, covering palette indices with and without a row-above predictor and a long-window zstd reference, to see how much of WebP's size advantage can be recovered at zstd speed.                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a palette-index mode for the lossless path, since it avoids the model assumption that failed for alpha-masked text. I'm also considering a per-block distinct-color count with an early exit to decide whether a     
 block goes to the lossy path, and I'm thinking about whether block-level intra copy with content hashes could help the repetitive text.                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now looking at the IBC side: rows could be folded into multi-row hashes over the scroll region's x-range, with solid rows discounted by multiplicity. Full-row repeats across list items are rare since the text differs, so  
 the real payoff is temporal reuse like scrolling back or re-entering a page, plus within-frame repeats of small elements such as icons, dividers and toggles.                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on A11y leaf nodes with image, switch, or checkbox classes and small bounds as the v1 sprite candidates, hashing their pixel rects as sprite IDs, and I'm leaving connected-component analysis for later glyph-level 
 evaluation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now weighing whether a sprite should be a tiny patch of rendered pixels keyed by hash. A sprite keeps its background, so it stays lossless and easy to check. The idea covers repeated toggles and back arrows, but it's a    
 separate gain from the page map, since sprites handle first-time content on unseen pages.                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether sprites actually save bytes over zstd, since a long-window zstd already catches repeated icon rows as short matches within a frame. The real gain is likely across frames and pages, where a sprite          
 reference is far cheaper than resending the pixels.                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the IDEA layer breakdown now: it names three layers, bg for layout, lit for the sprite pool, and fg for the video region. It also sorts regions into image, text, and video classes, which maps onto the lossy and   
 lossless paths I've been weighing.                                                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now checking how the IDEA layers map onto the region classes: bg, lit and fg each get their own quality setting, and I'm wondering whether a static photo thumbnail belongs in the lossy fg path or stays in bg with a lossy  
 encoder.                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether static images should sit in the lit sprite layer rather than fg, since the IDEA's three region classes (图/文/视) seem to map onto lit, bg and fg respectively. Keying image sprites by A11y ImageView       
 bounds and caching them by content hash would keep them out of the video layer, which fits the IDEA's reading better than GOAL's "image-like block → fg" mapping.                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now seeing that the image lossy path is the biggest byte lever, since images make up most of the bytes in the old corpus, yet GOAL schedules it in M5. I'm weighing whether the back-navigation frames, which include         
 launcher wallpaper exits, are inflating the page-cache gain.                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking how much of the back-frame byte share is really in scope, since the launcher wallpaper exits look like out-of-scope frames. Those frames would skew the stats, so the recorder should avoid pressing back at the     
 root or tag those frames as out of scope.                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm seeing that lossy image handling breaks the assumption behind the hash-verify scheme, since A's framebuffer no longer matches B's capture inside those rects. I'm weighing whether B should keep a reconstructed reference    
 frame, the way a video encoder does, and track the source and reconstructed hashes separately so the map still knows what A is showing.                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking how the hash-verify scheme survives lossy image rects, since A's pixels there won't match B's capture. Since B is the sole authority, A doesn't need source hashes for correctness, so the real check has to cover   
 only the lossless layers or compare against a reconstructed frame.                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the hashing rule for lossy content: row hashes for motion and IBC come from B's source pixels, so A never has to hash lossy output. Lossy rects get masked out of the debug verify hash, and A can decode them with  
 the browser's native decoders since any decoder variance stays out of the check.                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the JPEG encoder choice for image rects, weighing libjpeg-turbo speed against the Rust crates, and I'm treating the 4:2:0 chroma subsampling as a tunable trade-off for photos.                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how a partially visible image at the viewport edge should be encoded, since each newly exposed strip would become its own JPEG with seams and header overhead. The tall virtual capture helps here, so the plan   
 is to encode the whole image once it's captured rather than the visible slice.                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the rounded-corner edge case next: JPEG ringing over a flat background would show up at the corners, so I'm considering a lossless fix-up patch for those pixels.                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing how to keep B's JPEG encoding from needing A's decoded pixels, since browser decoders may differ slightly. One option is to split each image into a lossy interior and a lossless border ring, classifying 8×8 or    
 16×16 blocks by color count so flat background corners stay lossless.                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now weighing a three-layer split for image rects: 16×16 blocks get classified so flat background corners stay lossless, and the lossless blocks overdraw the lossy JPEG underneath. That hides the ringing at the rounded     
 corners, and the A11y ImageView bounds serve as a prior for the classification.                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether to cap the image ladder at two steps: a half-size or q≈35 preview first, then the target quality. The idea is that visible content gets a fast preview while refinement waits in the prefetch priority       
 order, as long as the target-quality byte estimate stays above the threshold.                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the rate budget next: at 300KB/s a 16ms frame carries only about 4.8KB, while a 100ms interaction window allows roughly 30KB, which matches the old steady-state target. I'm also checking whether browser           
 progressive decoding can deliver partial JPEG data early, though that adds complexity, so I'm leaning toward keeping the two-step ladder.                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing the first-page cost: at 300KB/s, even a compressed 71–153KB page takes a few hundred milliseconds before anything shows. That makes me think the order of delivery matters most, so I'm planning to send the chrome  
 and palette fills first, then text strips top to bottom, and images last in preview and then final quality. I'm also questioning whether the page should swap in atomically or stream in as independent patches.                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the first-page delivery now: a Page message carrying the background colour and a skeleton solid rect, so the tap gets immediate feedback instead of a half-second freeze. I'm also checking that congestion control  
 on a 300–800KB/s path won't queue visible patches behind stale data, which means B has to pace sends at the app level.                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now thinking about the pacing: rather than letting quinn's large default send window hide a backlog, I'd cap in-flight bytes at roughly 50–100ms of link rate, estimated from Ack timing. Stale visible patches should be     
 replaced at dequeue time, so the encoder works from what A will already have.                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now seeing that the encoder should be driven by the link's available credit rather than by capture: B diffs the latest frame against its model of what A has received and emits the most valuable patches only as far as the  
 link can carry. That lazy, demand-driven approach, similar to VNC's client-pull updates, keeps a slow link from building up latency, and I think it's a major gap in the current plan.                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing how to keep cross-stream ordering safe: a visible patch that copies from map content still in flight on the prefetch stream could arrive before its source. So the rule I'm leaning toward is that B only copies     
 from state A has already acknowledged, or from earlier on the same stream, accepting a small reuse delay for fewer reordering bugs.                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing two streams for visible and prefetch data against one stream with app-level scheduling. Loss on one stream wouldn't stall the other, so I'm leaning toward separate streams and making prefetch patches pure tile    
 writes outside the viewport.                                                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on the map-write rule: every write carries an increasing rev, and A only applies it if it's newer than what's stored for those rows, so cross-stream order stops mattering. I'm also noting that scroll positions    
 can go as absolute, idempotent ScrollTo values at 30–60Hz over datagrams, since the viewer composites scrolling locally and there's no high-rate touch stream to worry about.                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking how a tap gets routed when A's viewport and B's real scroll position have drifted apart. B would need to scroll first and then map the tap into its own coordinates. The main risk is tapping content A is still     
 showing from cache that B has already changed, so I'm thinking about verifying the rows around the tap point before sending it.                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the tap guard next: before injecting a tap, B compares the rows around the tap point against what A has, so a tap never lands on stale content like a delete button after the list has shifted. I'm also noting that 
 when the target row is inside the capture window, the tap maps straight to the tall display without needing a scroll. Then I'm thinking about the transient feedback: the ripple or pressed highlight that shows up for a few     
 milliseconds after a tap, which I'm planning to send as an overlay.                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether tap feedback should go through the encoded stream at all, since a ripple that finishes before the link has credit costs nothing if it's never sent. The open question is whether to spend limited bandwidth  
 on overlay animation or let A draw a simple local ripple instead.                                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now looking at whether Android's animator duration scale could switch off the ripple effect, since setting it to zero should make animations finish immediately. That would mean the tap feedback never shows up on screen,   
 which fits the plan's goal of keeping the default interface static.                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether the ripple feedback is worth the cost, and whether Android's animator duration scale would even affect it, though I'm not sure. I'm now thinking the caret blink can stay a simple two-state periodic sprite 
 that reuses the copy mechanism, costing about 10 bytes per toggle, so there's no need to synthesize it locally. I'm moving on to the scrollbar next, which I'm planning to treat as an overlay.                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm looking at the scrollbar now: it fades in during a scroll and fades out a few hundred milliseconds later, so its thumb shows up in the right-edge columns of every captured frame. That's why I'm cropping those columns out  
 of the row hashes. I also can't turn scrollbars off from B, since there's no global setting and the per-view switch isn't reachable.                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now working through how the scrollbar thumb would hide content in the right-edge strip. Since the thumb only covers part of that strip and moves much slower than the content, most rows should pass through visible,         
 thumb-free positions while they're on screen.                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how to pick the strip's pixels for each row when the scrollbar thumb sits over them. Rather than predicting the thumb from accessibility data, I'm thinking of detecting it from pixels: the strip is usually a   
 solid background and the thumb is a translucent gray shape, so I'd take the strip value from a frame where that row isn't under the thumb, or just extend the background column to its left.                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether the scrollbar strip can be handled without predicting where the thumb sits. The plan is to take those strip pixels only from observations where the thumb isn't drawn, and skip writing that strip while the 
 thumb is visible, with A drawing the thumb itself. I'm also looking at whether scrollbars can be turned off at the source, since no global setting exists for it.                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working through how the stretch overscroll would behave, since B could stop injecting scroll input once A11y reports it's at the top or bottom edge. The open question is whether a wheel injection that overshoots the edge  
 would still trigger the stretch effect.                                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now checking how RecyclerView handles edge glow for mouse-wheel input, recalling that it skips pulling glows when the event source is a mouse, so wheel injection shouldn't trigger the stretch overscroll. That would make   
 wheel injection a stronger actuator choice, though I still need to verify it in M0.                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm considering how the back stack could be tracked, mirroring page changes from window events and history navigation in the viewer. The risk is that Back at the root exits the app, so I'm thinking B should simply refuse to   
 inject Back when only one screen is open instead of relying on A to handle it.                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on the recovery approach for the root page: if a Back press makes the app's task disappear, B relaunches the app's root and repaints the cached root page, which is simpler than trying to predict whether Back will 
 exit. I'm also turning to the back stack as an IBC element, where each entry stores a page key and viewport anchor so a Back press can paint the previous page immediately from the map, before B's round trip completes.         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now going through the structure of the corpus: each device-date folder has a meta.jsonl with one line per frame, the per-app PNGs, and only sparse XML dumps that exist when the frame was captured with one.                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the corpus layout: the razr frames include side margins from a physical screen, while the xiaomi frames come from a 1080×2400 virtual display with mixed schemas, so some lines lack the color fields.           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm noting the corpus's timing problem: the frames have no timestamps, and the old doc showed the clock assumption alone shifts the pool contribution a lot. The captures are post-step snapshots rather than a continuous        
 stream, so intermediate animation and scrollbar-fade frames are missing, which means I can't evaluate overlay settling, prefetch scheduling, or latency from this data.                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm going through the corpus contents now: the XML dumps lack window lists, display IDs, and scroll events, and no scroll_step frame has one, so the scroll cross-checks can't be replayed. The scroll deltas are injected        
 command values rather than measured ones, and the random walk includes launcher and recovery frames I'll need to exclude.                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm looking at the corpus format now: each device-date folder has a meta.jsonl with one line per frame, PNGs per app, and sparse XML dumps. I'm going to suggest the new format record raw frames from the real pipeline with     
 monotonic timestamps, so the encoder can be replayed at the recorded times.                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm noting how the corpus stores each trace as a plain input script, with taps keyed by resource-id or text rather than raw coordinates so it stays portable across devices. I'm also looking at frame storage: PNG decoding  
 is slow and a long continuous capture would be huge, so I'm weighing delta-compressed frames or content-addressed unique frames instead.                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a content-addressed store of zstd-compressed raw frames, which would dedupe the many identical frames, against lossless video via ffmpeg, which brings a dependency and color-space risks. I lean toward the simpler 
 raw-frame option, since it's straightforward to implement in Rust on both the recording and replay sides.                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing the storage rate for the on-device recording: raw 1080×2400 frames at 60fps would be about 600MB/s, which is too much, so I'm considering dedupe and zstd-1 on only the dirty rows, with a rough estimate of roughly 
 30MB/s that looks workable for UFS.                                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing how to record the phone side cheaply: raw frames at 60fps would be far too much data, so I'm considering compressing only the changed rows and streaming them to the host over adb forward. I'd expect that to fit   
 within the storage and CPU budget, though the recorder could drop frames if it's CPU-limited, and I'm noting that recording itself perturbs timing, so latency should come from live runs rather than recordings.                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm laying out what the event log should capture: a single monotonic timestamp on every record, covering frames, inputs, tree dumps, window and IME changes, and markers. Frames would reference their content hash, and the      
 accessibility tree and its events would carry the fields needed to replay scrolling and collection state.                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm going through the scenarios the algorithm has to cover, since the random walk doesn't hit them well: long scroll down and back up, entering subpages and backing out several levels, returning to a page after leaving the    
 app, repeated switch toggles, tab switching, editor typing with IME state, dialogs, scrollbar drags, variable-height lists, image-heavy scrolling, and one more case I haven't finished listing.                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm noting that the corpus plan references a node-based script location, so I'll check whether that path is still accurate before recommending where the new traces should live.                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now looking at the network side of the comparison: I'd shape the link with tc netem, either on the loopback or the adb-forward path, so both scrcpy and our stream see identical bandwidth and delay. The metrics I'm         
 weighing are total bytes, peak bytes in any one-second window, time to the first and last settled pixel after an input, pixel difference against ground truth, and stall time. The old doc cuts off at that last line, so I'm     
 leaving its specifics aside.                                                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out the metrics for the comparison, starting with the per-interaction byte totals and peaks, then the completion time under a fixed link rate, since that folds bytes into latency for the 300–800KB/s target. Next   
 I'm considering blank-row time during scrolls for prefetch, and on-device encode timing.                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    I'm now thinking about the offline bench, which needs a viewer model with discrete-event simulation over link rate, RTT, and the scheduler to measure blank-rate, and I'd move the scheduler into a pure Rust function so the     
 simulator and live host share it. I'm also noting that ablation flags should be an independent bitset in the encoder config, with the bench reporting how each feature's removal changes bytes and encode time.                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now weighing oracle upper bounds before committing to any feature: an "oracle dedupe" bound for map and IBC, and an "oracle static" bound for literal coding with the strongest lossless compressor. Old doc's glyph-sprite   
 gain could be checked offline with connected-component hashing first.                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether glyph-level sprites can work here: pixel-exact connected-component hashing keeps output exact, but Android usually places text at integer positions without subpixel flags, so identical glyphs should       
 dedupe well.                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm estimating what glyph-level sprites would actually save on CJK text. Each character breaks into several connected components, so I'd need line-box grouping, and each glyph reference costs only about 3–4 bytes against      
 roughly 150–300 bytes for a first-seen glyph, which means the gain depends on how often characters repeat.                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working through why the glyph-sprite gain could be worth about 2× on repeated-text pages, since each repeated glyph costs roughly 100 bytes as zstd sequences versus about 4 bytes as a sprite reference. That makes the      
 upper bound worth computing offline with the oracle approach before I commit to the feature, and I'm moving on to the residual dirty-rect encoding next.                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether a zstd dictionary built from the previous frame's pixels would work, but only if both sides hold byte-identical lossless content, so lossy rectangles would have to be zeroed out on both ends. That also    
 means B would need to keep actual pixel data for the reference rather than just hashes.                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether a zstd dictionary built from the previous frame's pixels would be workable on the WASM side, since the usual C binding needs a wasm toolchain I haven't verified. A pure-Rust decoder like ruzstd might      
 avoid that, so I'm looking at whether it supports the dictionary mode I need.                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether zstd-sys can build for wasm32-unknown-unknown through its shim, and I'll mark that as a milestone check. I'm also weighing whether zstd is even the right back-end for palette index planes, compared with a 
 context-modeling arithmetic coder.                                                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a "copy-above" transform for palette indices, where a pixel equal to the one above becomes zero, so vertical repetition turns into zero runs that zstd compresses well. The palette could also be sorted by          
 luminance so that the predictive filters make sense for anti-aliased ramps.                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now weighing a copy-above transform for the palette indices, checking it against plain indices and a luma-sorted palette with the Up filter across a few zstd levels, so the bench picks the winner. Next I'm looking at the  
 per-tile hash for the dirty-rect check. At around 7ms per tall frame it eats a large share of a core at 60fps, so I'm considering skipping hashing when no new frame arrives.                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the per-frame cost of row hashing, which the old doc put at roughly 0.7 to 0.5 ms per step. Comparing the previous frame row by row first should keep hashing limited to dirty rows, so it isn't the bottleneck.     
 Hashing in place with the row stride would avoid an extra copy. Since tall mode multiplies the ImageReader buffer memory, I'd drop maxImages to 2 or 3.                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the last part of the dirty-rect work: hashing only dirty rows keeps the cost down, and hashing in place with the row stride avoids an extra copy. I'd also drop the buffer count to 2 or 3 in tall mode, since the   
 memory cost grows with the height factor.                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking how the WebUI gets served from localhost on the PC side, since the page needs to be a secure context to connect to the Tailscale address with a cert hash. I'm considering a simple static file server and passing   
 the host address, port, and token through the URL fragment.                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on localhost for the WebUI, with the host address, cert hash, and token passed in the URL fragment. For the certificate, B prints a fresh URL each time the daemon starts, and I'd regenerate the cert around the    
 seven-day mark and push the next hash to A over the live connection. I'll also backdate notBefore by a day to absorb clock skew between the phone and the PC.                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on the token going in the URL fragment so it never reaches the server logs or a Referer header. For a phone as viewer, localhost would need a local server on the device, so I'm weighing a publicly hosted https    
 page instead, which also supports the certificate hash check. That leaves an open question about how the phone-side WebUI should be served.                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now thinking about how to persist the per-page map on the viewer side, using OPFS with segment files and an index. Since synchronous access handles only work in a Worker, the WASM decoder and storage belong in a dedicated 
 Worker, leaving the main thread to handle input, and I'm weighing how cache-revision bumps should invalidate stored data.                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on a render-environment hash to namespace the cache, built from width, density, font scale, night mode, locale, and app version. Without it, stale pages from an app update or a dark-mode switch would never get    
 hit and would just waste storage. Hash verification still keeps the wrong pixels off screen, but speculative paints from a stale environment could flash the wrong content, so the namespace is worth including.                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how persisted cache entries should store their data. Storing decoded pixels would be wasteful, so I'm leaning toward saving the encoded tile bodies keyed by page, region, row and revision, as long as each  
 one decodes on its own without depending on outside references.                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on how persisted segments get encoded on the viewer side, since the stored tiles can't just be the received patches when a Copy op has been resolved into pixels. Options include a WASM zstd compressor, the        
 browser's built-in deflate stream, or a small custom codec, and I'm leaning toward the shared Rust zstd for simplicity.                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the A-side persistence model: lossless map strips get re-encoded for storage, while image sprites are kept as the original received blobs, referenced by id from the map. That splits the cache into three layers:   
 background strips, content-addressed sprites, and untouched video.                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm planning how the memory budgets work on the phone: a RAM cache for decoded pixels, plus a compressed on-disk cache with LRU eviction by last visit. On the PC side I'm keeping a small index per page that just tracks   
 segment hashes and revisions.                                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now weighing the milestone order: the Kotlin host capture and recorder have to come first, then an offline bench against a scrcpy-style H.264 baseline, with the full-run size, timing, and peak-memory scripts added later.  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm comparing the bitrate and latency against a scrcpy baseline, running the same drag trace on a scrcpy virtual display since it can't mirror ours directly. I might also feed the recorded raw frames through x264 for an       
 offline apples-to-apples check.                                                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing how to benchmark the encoder against scrcpy: the same drag trace on a scrcpy virtual display, plus offline x264 on the recorded raw frames for a deterministic check, with the headline number coming from the live  
 run. For quality at matched bitrate, I'd compare time until a frame is pixel-exact or above 45 dB PSNR after an interaction, and the fraction of pixels still differing once it settles.                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now covering how A's eviction affects B's view of the cache: when A drops entries, B's model goes stale, so A will report evictions and B will resend whatever a missing reference points to. A's speculative paints don't    
 depend on B at all.                                                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working through how the edge bands at the top and bottom of a scroll region get handled. Shadows from the toolbar and fading edges make those rows differ from the pure content, so I'm considering detecting them when a     
 scroll's interior rows verify but the edge rows don't, and learning per-page edge insets to store with the page. The pixels in those bands blend content with the shadow, so the viewer can't cleanly separate them.              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now checking a consequence of decoupling: B captures frames at its own positions, so the exact viewport offset A is showing may never be confirmed, leaving the edge-band rows without an exact patch.                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the idle behavior: once the viewer stops scrolling, B shifts its real offset to match A's viewport, so the edge bands and chrome become exact pixels and A's canvas converges to the true frame at rest.             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out what the display looks like at rest: the toolbar sits at the top, the scroll region runs between the chrome, and the bottom bar anchors to the tall display's bottom. Floating elements like the FAB and snackbar 
 are positioned from that bottom edge, so I'm checking how they land relative to the tall window.                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how the bottom-anchored overlays like the FAB should be composited when the viewport sits at the tall display's bottom, since their pixels mix with list content beneath them. Cutting them out by their          
 accessibility bounds leaves rounded corners showing the wrong background, so exact matting would be needed. I'm checking whether IDEA's enabling condition, a full-width bottom bar or a scroll region reaching the screen        
 bottom, avoids that mixing.                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm adding a rule that pages with a floating element like the FAB, which sits above a list but isn't full-width, should turn off tall mode or have that element cut out with a known flaw. Next I'm considering how content       
 changes after load, like image placeholders being swapped for thumbnails, which would bump the tile revision.                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now looking at how B's encoding cost compares to the link: B's CPU isn't the bottleneck, so spending 20–50ms to save about 30% of the bytes at 300KB/s is worth it, unlike the old LAN design that rejected high zstd levels. 
 Since encoding happens at send time, the compression level can adapt to the queue.                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing the cost of encoding effort against the link: at 300 KB/s, spending about 30 ms more on a higher zstd level to save roughly 16% of a 150 KB page's bytes comes out ahead, since that saves around 78 ms of           
 transmission.                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the bitrate tradeoff with the old numbers: a 157 KB text page at zstd-3 drops to 126 KB at zstd-9, about 20% smaller. Even the WebP lossless option, which cuts it to 71 KB but costs around 196 ms to encode, still 
 comes out ahead on this link, breaking even only near 439 KB/s.                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the break-even point for the encoding tradeoff: using the old numbers, a WebP lossless encode costs about 190ms more than zstd-3 on a text page, so it only pays off below roughly 450KB/s. Since the link is the    
 bottleneck at 300KB/s, the compression level should adapt to the send backlog. I'm also noting that under credit-driven sending, peak throughput is fixed by the link rate, so time-to-complete and backlog duration are the more 
 useful metrics. Next I'm going back through GOAL.md against IDEA.md to find what's outdated.                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the whitelist behavior against IDEA: the plan needs enforcement, since launching an activity could bring up an app outside the whitelist. I'm noting that the installer UI from an APK install would fall outside it 
 too, so the foreground package needs to be watched.                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the whitelist enforcement next: if the foreground package falls outside the list, the output should blank and navigate back, since an activity launcher in the list could open arbitrary apps. I'm also going        
 through the IDEA input mappings to confirm that keys, clicks, wheel, back, and clipboard already line up with GOAL's messages, and I'm noting that text input needs an IME policy on the virtual display.                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the display's input handling next: the virtual display should hide the soft keyboard so it doesn't eat a big chunk of the screen and bytes, and non-ASCII text would have to go through clipboard paste instead of   
 key events. I'm also noting that the display should run without system decorations, so no status bar or notifications show up.                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the remaining IDEA items against GOAL: the display should run without system decorations, so there's no status bar to reserve space for. I'm also flagging a verification item for M0: whether the virtual display   
 keeps producing frames once the physical screen turns off, since IDEA expects the host to be able to sleep its screen.                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm considering a cheaper way to estimate shadow encoding than encoding everything twice: track the average bytes per pixel for literal coding by content class from what was actually sent, then multiply by the pixels saved,   
 with exact shadow coding reserved for offline ablation. I also want per-app tunables, like the heuristics the left-side panel exposes, published by the encoder so they can be inspected.                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking IDEA's remaining items against GOAL: the per-app tunables should be published by the encoder and carried over as protocol messages rather than HTTP, and the SDK setup and one-liner examples need to go into the    
 README and M0 exit criteria. I'm also noting that the long-screenshot debugging should export from the map, as the old version did.                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the dev path for the WebTransport-only design, since adb forward only carries TCP and can't relay QUIC. The old setup reached the phone over its LAN IP instead, so I'm weighing a dev flag that binds that address, 
 or moving the host's network part onto the PC with capture linked over adb.                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether the virtual display can keep rendering after the physical screen turns off, since the host needs to be able to sleep its screen. For the dev path, I'm binding the WebTransport server to the Wi-Fi LAN IP   
 behind a dev flag instead of 0.0.0.0, and adding a PC replay host that feeds recorded sessions through the same host-net crate.                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm double-checking the sendOrder claim: it only applies to streams the client creates, so for the B-to-A direction I'd need to set priority on the server's send stream instead. Next I'm confirming the quinn default MTU upper 
 bound and the RecyclerView details against the docs.                                                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the RecyclerView source next, specifically how mouse input triggers pullGlows and how CollectionItemInfoCompat and setFromIndex are used.
