 I'm mapping the three image/text/video mask classes onto the layers: text goes to the background layer as lossless palette content, images to the lossy sprite layer, and video to the foreground. That means GOAL's rule of      
 treating image-like blocks as foreground conflicts with this split, and the plan needs fixing.                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling how to label the layers against the content classes: text goes to the background layer as lossless palette content, images to the sprite pool as content-addressed items, and video alone to the foreground, so      
 GOAL's habit of sending image-like blocks to fg needs to change.                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking how the wire-level priority should work: the sendOrder idea in GOAL.md is a browser-side setting for outgoing streams, so downlink ordering would have to be set on the server's send streams instead.               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how prefetch should handle consistency: if a prefetch stream is reset, B can't be sure A received those tiles, so B should only treat tiles as held by A once they're acknowledged, keeping in-flight ones        
 separate. The open question is ordering across streams, since a visible patch on its own stream might reference a tile still travelling on the prefetch stream.                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking where GOAL's plan departs from the design: visible-stream patches can only reference tiles already on that same stream or tiles the client has acknowledged, since a visible patch might otherwise arrive before the 
 prefetch tile it depends on. I'm also noting that tap coordinates have to be mapped back into the content position, which means the capture head must scroll first, adding latency.                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the claim that a wheel injection gives exact displacement: RecyclerView handles pointer-source vertical scroll immediately, with no touch slop and no fling, so the scroll lands deterministically.                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the claim that mouse-wheel injection moves a RecyclerView exactly, since it skips touch slop and fling entirely, which would be a cleaner alternative to drag injection. The catch is that only some containers      
 handle generic motion events, and the pixel step depends on the scaled vertical scroll factor, so I need to see how the axis value maps to pixels on a given density.                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether mouse-wheel injection could replace drag injection for moving the capture head, since it would skip touch slop and fling. The catch is that not every container handles generic motion events, and I'd need  
 to confirm whether recent Android versions add smooth scrolling to wheel input, so that gets checked in M0 with the old Wheel and Scroll measurements as the comparison.                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Next I'm weighing a third route: the accessibility action for scrolling to a given position, which LinearLayoutManager exposes on newer Android versions, plus forward and backward page scrolls that may animate.                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking how RecyclerView reports position: it only passes scroll deltas, not an absolute offset, so cumulative error would build up. But each item exposes its adapter position through accessibility node info, so pairing  
 that position with the item's bounds could give a stable per-item anchor.                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a global pixel strip for the content position against tiles keyed by item index and offset within the item. The item-anchored version handles variable heights and reentry without relocating from the first screen, 
 but accessibility positions lag, so I'd treat them as hints and confirm them with row hashes. The global version is simpler, yet it drifts whenever a frame is lost, so the question is whether exact wheel deltas make that      
 drift small enough to accept.                                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm thinking about how to anchor the content position: item index plus offset within the item might be sturdier than a global pixel strip, since A11y row indices and item counts would let me estimate total height for a        
 synthetic scrollbar. The catch is that those accessibility values can lag, so they would only serve as hints for relocation, with row hashes still doing the confirmation.                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a tall virtual display as the core of the prefetch method: the app lays out on a taller surface than the visible one, so content beyond the screen edge is already rendered, and the scroll region picks up the      
 extra height when its bottom sits flush with the screen.                                                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing the tall virtual display for prefetch: the app lays out on a taller surface, so the scroll window shows local scroll for free. The open problems are that resizing can trigger a config change or state loss, so 
 I'd keep the tall display fixed for the whole session, and that pages without a single scroll region plus a pinned bottom bar won't fit this method.                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether a tall virtual display should apply to every page, since centered dialogs, bottom sheets, and a calculator keypad would all be stretched or mispositioned on a taller surface. That points toward enabling   
 it per single page rather than for the whole session.                                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether resizing the virtual display per page is safe, since a resize changes the reported screen height and can trigger a configuration change that recreates the activity or drops state. Apps that handle those   
 config changes themselves would survive it, but the rest would not, so I'd need to check which pages declare that handling before enabling the tall display for them.                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a fixed tall display for the whole session, but that leaves non-scroll pages like centered dialogs and bottom-anchored content sitting in the wrong place on a taller surface.                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm considering a third option: instead of resizing the virtual display, change the task's window bounds, for example through freeform mode or launch bounds. That would keep the display size fixed, though I'd still need to    
 see how the app responds to bounds changes.                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm noting that every variant still makes the app see a config change, since resizing the task's bounds has the same effect as resizing the display. I can cut the display reconfiguration cost with the task-bounds route, but   
 I'd still need to check whether apps that don't handle configChanges survive it.                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing per-app tall display from session start, since that avoids resizing mid-session, but pages that don't suit the method, like calendar grids and calculator keypads, would be stretched to the taller height, so I'm   
 checking which whitelisted apps have such root pages.                                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether to resize the display per page or per app: per page avoids a tall layout on non-scroll screens, but each resize may trigger a config change, so I'd check whether the app's activity already declares those  
 config changes as handled and resize freely only for those.                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on a per-app check: whether the activity already declares screen-size config changes as handled, which PackageManager can report. If it does, resizing the display for a page is cheap, since nothing gets           
 relaunched. Height is the only dimension likely to change, because the width stays fixed and the phone is already in landscape-long layout.                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether resizing is cheap enough to do per page: if an activity already declares screen-size config changes as handled, a resize won't relaunch it. Otherwise I'd fall back to a height fixed for the whole session. 
 On a first visit, I won't know whether a page qualifies until the accessibility dump arrives a moment later, so the page shows at normal height first and then relayouts. The top rows should stay the same, so the row-hash      
 comparison should stay cheap.                                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the cost of a tall frame: three times the pixels means roughly 31 MB per RGBA capture and about 7 ms of row hashing, and the app would also bind three times as many list items, with a possible texture-size limit  
 to watch for.                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Checking whether the GPU's max texture size covers a 1080×7200 frame, since most modern mobile GPUs support at least 8192 but I'm not certain about the exact limit on this hardware. Since the plan already allows roughly a     
 3–4× height increase, the bigger concern is how much each captured frame costs to diff, so I'm considering whether hardware buffers from ImageReader could help limit comparisons to the damaged region.                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how to batch the capture head: with a tall display, each capture gives extra lookahead rows at once, so the head should jump by roughly the tall scroll height minus an overlap kept for anchor verification,     
 rather than moving strip by strip.                                                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm looking at how to keep the scrollbar out of the captured frames: its thumb fades in and out while scrolling, so the right-edge columns would change pixel by pixel on every frame.                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling how the scrollbar fade affects when tiles can be committed: it's driven by a delayed callback and a fade duration from ViewConfiguration rather than by ValueAnimator, so the animator duration scale won't shorten

 I'm trying to tell the thin scrollbar column apart from real content: without the accessibility tree exposing the thumb, I'd have to locate it from pixels, treating a narrow band along the right edge as scrollbar. For the     
 tile content, I'd rebuild those edge pixels from frames where the thumb sits elsewhere, since each content row should appear at more than one thumb position if the overlap is large enough.                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on scrolling as the simplest robust approach: let the edge band be handled as its own channel rather than mixed into the tile body. Since the thumb moves at a different rate than the content, each row should show 
 up in multiple captures with the thumb in different places, which makes it possible to choose a clean band without over-engineering the comparison.                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on two kinds of tile state: provisional ones, where the edge band is filled from the neighbouring background column and shown right away, and settled ones, which are confirmed exact by hash comparison and are the 
 only ones persisted. A settle pass later corrects whatever the provisional fill got wrong.                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on two kinds of tile state for each map cell, provisional or exact, and the grid can show which is which. Images stay lossy at the chosen quality unless a lossless setting is picked. Next I'm working out how to   
 detect the bottom bar, as a full-width node anchored to the bottom edge that the scroll region stops short of.                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how to classify the non-scroll nodes, like the bottom bar and any bottom-anchored floating buttons. The idea is to compare the layout at two heights: nodes whose top edge stays put are top-anchored, nodes      
 whose distance from the bottom stays put are bottom-anchored, and nodes that change size are the stretching scroll region.                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether the scroll region stretches or just shifts when the page gets taller, since that decides whether the two-height layout comparison can tell the nodes apart.                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether a floating button that overlaps the scroll content can be reconstructed exactly, since its shadow blends semi-transparently with whatever list rows sit beneath it. Two options are on the table: exclude    
 pages where bottom-anchored elements overlap the scrolling region from the tall mode, falling back to normal height with head-scrolling prefetch, or accept approximate provisional pixels for those spots.                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on the clean-capture idea: rows under a fixed overlay like the FAB get excluded, so the usable strip is the scroll region minus roughly the bottom 100dp.                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm looking at how the scrollable-region overlays and collapsing toolbars affect the capture: a collapsing app bar moves by a different amount than the list beneath it during the first part of a scroll, so there are two       
 displacement regions rather than one rigid shift. The old "multiple shift rounds" handling may need to cover that, and the Settings homepage is a likely real case to check.                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking how the app bar and the list move during a wheel-injected scroll. CollapsingToolbarLayout shrinks the title as it collapses while the content beneath scrolls rigidly, so the header region isn't a simple shift and 
 the capture has to account for that.                                                                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm considering how to model the app bar's collapse, since its header changes non-rigidly and can't be reproduced locally from pixels. One option is to treat that collapsing range as a region where the viewer falls back to    
 showing the real remote frames, and only composites locally once the scroll is rigid with a pinned toolbar. The other is to snap the expanded state into a prefix tile.                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether to treat the collapsing header as a non-rigid region where the viewer shows the real remote frames, or to snap the expanded header into a prefix tile. Either way, only the settled picture at each scroll   
 position has to match what the app would show, since the in-between frames are already viewer-generated.                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on a rest reconciliation step: during motion the viewport stays provisional, and once scrolling stops the capture head moves to the same position and compares hashes, patching only on mismatch. With rigid maps    
 that check passes with no bytes sent, but I'm not yet sure how it holds up when the tall layout differs from what a normal-height app would show.                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the rest state as the reference: once scrolling stops, the composite should match B's tall frame at the same position. The capture window only has to contain A's viewport, not line up with it exactly, so the head 
 doesn't need to move much.                                                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how a tap should map back to the remote display: the viewport position converts to a content offset, then to a point on the remote screen relative to its current head. If that point falls inside the capture    
 window, which holds at rest, the tap can go straight through; if a tap lands mid-motion and the target is outside the window, the head has to move first.                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working through the tap-rejection rule: a tap gets refused with a stale signal if the page epoch has changed or the target rows aren't confirmed equal on the capture side. I'm also starting a fourth point about events     
 where the app scrolls on its own, like when the keyboard appears.                                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the default for static interfaces: B doesn't re-verify content when scrolling back or returning, unless a page is set to live, and it trusts the cache. Pages that do change still get checked, since B keeps        
 capturing and hashing rows, so any row that differs from the map gets sent as a diff.                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the "what counts as the answer" question: at rest, the viewer's picture should match what the app would show at that scroll position, and the cached pages are shown right away and only checked against what the    
 capture window sees. I'm also separating the cache version, which changes with the codec, display geometry, or theme, from a per-page revision counter that lets the capture side send only the differences.                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling how the last piece of the page map gets tracked: each segment records the revision at which it last changed, so a diff is just the segments newer than what the viewer already holds. The open question is what      
 happens if the viewer's revision runs ahead of the capture side's, meaning the capture side lost its state and only kept hashes.                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on content-addressed storage for the page map: each segment is keyed by its hash and held in a blob store, so B only needs to send a manifest of ranges and hashes when it enters a page, and A can fetch whatever   
 blobs it lacks.                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether to keep a persisted hash record on the capture side at all, or to have it compute segment hashes fresh whenever it enters a page and send those as the manifest.                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether A should be the single persistent owner of the page cache, with B's session state rebuilt from A's inventory, or whether B should keep its own persisted hash record alongside the revision counter.         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the cache key scheme: a cache_rev derived from codec version, display size and density, font scale, night mode, and locale, so that a change in any of those keeps a separate namespace instead of wiping the cache. 
 Per-app state would track the package's version code and last update time, and a pg_rev would be a per-page counter that B assigns within its store generation.                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm sketching the protocol messages now: a Hello with the cache and page revisions, a Pages reply after opening a package, and on page entry a Page message that carries only a revision check. If the revisions differ, the      
 capture side sends a manifest of segment hashes for whatever changed since the viewer's revision, and the viewer answers by hash from its blob store, with a miss reply for anything it lacks.                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how to key each page: the plan is to hash the accessibility tree's structure with list contents stripped out, so a page is identified by its layout rather than its data.                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether a page can be identified by its accessibility skeleton with list contents removed, since my corpus check found a few collisions. The settings sub-pages look like the risk: they'd likely share the same

 I'm checking whether a page key built from the accessibility skeleton holds up, since the Settings sub-pages likely share one toolbar-plus-recycler layout and would collide. I'm thinking of adding a discriminator from the

 I'm settling on tap-driven navigation: the back button can restore the previous page from the recorded stack with high confidence, while forward taps would be predicted from a learned graph that links each page to the pages   
 its taps have led to.                                                                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether the tapped item should be the key for remembering navigation, so that a later tap on the same row could jump straight to the page it led to before. The hard part is that the pixel side doesn't know which  
 accessibility node was tapped, so I'm considering keying each edge by the page and a hash of the tapped row's pixels instead.                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how taps become edges: each tap result records a navigation from one page to another, tied to the clickable rect it hit. A later tap inside a known rect could switch pages optimistically, with B confirming 
 or correcting afterward. I'm also checking whether forward optimism is worth the risk of a wrong-page flash, and whether going this far goes beyond what the original idea asked for.                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the largest byte sinks against the old measurements, since the back-navigation share of 48.6% includes the launcher wallpaper that appears when leaving the app from its root page.                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at how much of the old byte total is out of scope: the back-navigation frames include launcher wallpaper, and about 21 of 87 back frames have more than 20,000 colours, which is wallpaper-like. Since the        
 session is single-app, those frames should be flagged as recording errors or tagged in_scope=false so they don't pollute the baseline.                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Weighing lossy image encoding now: the image literals are about 73% of the old byte total, so that's the biggest lever. For Android, libjpeg-turbo with NEON could encode a full-screen frame in roughly 15–25 ms on a big core,  
 with the browser decoding it natively and off-thread, whereas lossy WebP would be several times slower to encode.                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing lossy encoders for the image literals, which make up about 73% of the old bytes. JPEG via libjpeg-turbo looks fast enough for a full-screen frame on a big core, and the browser can decode it natively off-thread,  
 while WebP lossy would be considerably slower to encode. I'm also checking whether Android's own Bitmap compression could avoid native dependencies, though I'm not sure the runtime initialises graphics in app_process.         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing JPEG against other lossy options for the image literals: libjpeg-turbo with NEON looks fast enough on a big core, though I still need to check whether browsers decode JPEG with identical pixels, since any     
 difference would break determinism on A's side.                                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing the image layer: the rounded icon corners blend image and background, so a lossy encode of the full rect would ring at the corners. My thought is to encode the rect lossy and then correct the non-image pixels 
 exactly with a lossless mask boundary.                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm thinking about the mask for rounded icons: pixels exactly matching the background get restored from the background layer, while the anti-aliased edge stays in the lossy image, so the mask is just a cheap run-length    
 bitmap.                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether a deterministic codec in the shared Rust crate would let both sides agree on image pixels, which would matter if refinement depends on exact decoded values.                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a near-lossless integer codec in the shared Rust crate, with quantised residuals bounding the error to a small fixed amount, so both sides would agree on the decoded pixels and sharp edges would survive.          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing a two-rung ladder for the image layer: a JPEG-class lossy encode first to hit the bandwidth target, since thumbnails drop roughly tenfold at q80, with an optional near-lossless refinement at idle when that    
 tunable is on.                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm considering small icons: at 48dp they're only about 4–6 KB as JPEG, and since the accessibility tree gives each ImageView's bounds, those rects make natural sprite boundaries. Identical icons, like the same icon       
 repeated for each activity of one app, could be deduplicated by a content hash against the literal pool.                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing a palette-and-index approach for the text and symbolic parts: classify each ImageView rect by colour count, treating few-colour, single-hue rects as symbolic and encoding them losslessly, and leaving

 Now I'm checking how glyph sprites would work: copying exact bitmap connected components, as opposed to re-rendering fonts, is a different approach, and the earlier measured gain for it was only about 8.4%, so it's a low

 Now I'm checking whether zstd's long window already captures repeated glyph bitmaps, and it mostly doesn't, since glyph rows interleave in raster order. A palette-index map with 2D back-references, copying from the row above

 Now I'm planning the remaining dirty-rectangle fallback: zstd, possibly with a prediction filter and a long window, or with the previous frame's pixels at the same position as a dictionary. That covers small changes like a    
 toggle or counter, where a delta against the prior frame should compress well.                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out the background layer: a page-level palette of primary and surface tones, shared across tiles so each tile only references indices rather than resending colours. For anti-aliased text edges, I'd code each   
 pixel as a blend of two palette colours with a small alpha, and fall back to an escape literal wherever the rounding doesn't reproduce the exact pixel.                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on a plain per-tile palette of up to 256 colours with an index map compressed by zstd, with indices ordered by luminance so predictive filters work better. That should capture most of the benefit of an alpha      
 model without depending on exact blend reproduction.                                                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling on a palette-based approach for the background and text: a per-tile palette of up to 256 colours, sorted by luminance so the index map compresses well, which covers anti-aliased edges without needing an exact 
 blend model. I'm also keeping in mind that the encoder has to simulate the decoder, so the sender always knows exactly what state the receiver holds.

 Now I'm noting that the accessibility tree is a hint rather than ground truth, since it lags, so I'll use it to guide where to look and let the pixels verify. Fetching it isn't free either: walking the nodes over binder IPC

 I'm weighing how to treat the display's input policy: the IME should stay off the virtual screen so it doesn't pop up or cover the content, and on a touch-only device I'd need a hidden input field in the WebUI to bring up its

 I'm checking whether the virtual display flags hold up on the device: trusted, own-focus, always-unlocked, and an own display group so the host can turn its screen off without stopping the capture. Scrcpy's flag set is the

 Now I'm working out the rate budget: at 300–800 KB/s, a text-heavy list page of roughly 150 KB takes about 0.2–0.5 s to send, so prefetch has to stay under whatever bandwidth the visible content isn't using, and frames should 
 be coalesced so a newer one replaces an unsent older one instead of queuing behind it.                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how the encoder paces itself: it encodes the freshest frame only once the send window has room, measured against what A has already confirmed, so slow links skip stale frames at the source.                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how to spend the limited link: order the visible text and layout first, then low-quality images, then the prefetch, with QUIC stream priorities kept to about three levels since many levels hurt             
 performance. On a link around 1280 bytes MTU, I'll also account for IP and UDP header overhead when sizing the packets.                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out the MTU: on a Tailscale link at 1280 bytes, that leaves about 1252 bytes of UDP payload over IPv4 and 1232 over IPv6, and QUIC's 1200-byte minimum still fits. I'm also checking quinn's discovery probes,    
 which would mostly be lost above that limit, so I'm considering capping the upper bound near 1252 for an IPv6 interface.                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling the MTU question: on a 1280-byte Tailscale path, the usable UDP payload is about 1252 over IPv4 and 1232 over IPv6, so I'd set the upper bound at 1232 and keep the initial MTU at 1200. Raising it from 1200 to 
 1232 only buys about 2.7%, so I'm inclined to simply turn MTU discovery off.

 I'm working out why tall capture doesn't help the network side: the head can only move a couple thousand pixels per frame, far faster than the link can carry, so raw scroll speed isn't the bottleneck.                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether the tall display is worth it at all: it would let the head prefetch more rows per frame and lead without moving, but it brings config-change, extra-loading, and dialog-placement costs. A tap would mean    
 scrolling back into position first, which should only add a frame or two of latency, as long as the content at that position hasn't changed.                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a tall virtual display that would be turned on per page, since the gold-standard approach defaults it on for single pages whose scroll region reaches the bottom of the screen. Rather than contradict that          
 silently, I'd keep it but measure it as an ablation with tall-display factors of 1x, 2x and 3x, and possibly decide the height at launch for each app.                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a resize at page-transition time, when the new page is being pushed anyway, and restoring the previous size on back. I'd also cache a per-layout "tall-safe" flag, blacklisting it if the Activity recreates or      
 scroll position is lost. Before trusting a resize, I'd compare the top rows against the pre-resize frame to confirm the header and scroll content still match.                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the fallback for IME handling on the virtual display: by default the virtual display's keyboard shows on the default screen, so I want it hidden to keep typed input from being routed there.                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now looking at how to make the row-based image-change detection less brittle, since a single changed pixel such as a scrollbar, ripple, or badge would make a whole 1080-wide row miss. I'm considering splitting each scroll 
 row into several column bands aligned to the accessibility item boundaries, so a local change only invalidates its own band.                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm thinking about splitting each scroll row into several column bands, so a change in one area such as a trailing switch doesn't break the whole row's match. The band edges would come from the accessibility item bounds,  
 so the hashes stay stable.                                                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at glyph-level sprites as a way to make the text-heavy list pages cheaper. The earlier offline result showed about an 8.4% gain on text-heavy pages, but anti-aliased glyphs drawn at different subpixel offsets  
 produce different pixels, so exact-match deduplication would miss them.                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm considering how glyph-level sprites would behave on Android text: with subpixel positioning, Skia likely quantizes each glyph to a few horizontal offsets, so deduplicating connected components would grow the dictionary by 
 a small factor rather than break entirely.                                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm thinking about glyph-level sprites again: Skia likely quantizes subpixel positions to a few offsets, so the dictionary should grow only modestly, which I'd want to confirm by measuring connected-component hit rates. CJK   
 text is harder, since Chinese characters split into several components and the distinct-character count is large, so I'm considering segmenting by accessibility text node bounds and strings instead.                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm looking at using each character's bounding box from the accessibility tree to cut text into per-glyph cells, so I don't need connected-component analysis. Each cell would be keyed by a hash of its quantized pixels, with   
 the codepoint only serving as a prediction hint, and unmatched cells falling back to a literal mask.                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether glyph sprites still pay off across pages, since text repeated on other pages can be cached persistently so that new pages cost only about two bytes per character.                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether the Android accessibility API's per-character location extra data is available on the relevant API levels, since exact character boxes would let me cut text into glyph cells without connected-component

 I'm considering a simpler baseline for glyph-level savings: text-line and item-level sprites, compressed with zstd against a persistent per-app dictionary trained on earlier pages. That would avoid the glyph segmentation      
 problem while still capturing much of the gain.                                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm thinking about making glyph sprites work with LZ77-style compression: if each glyph's pixels are laid out contiguously within a text-line strip, repeated glyphs would show up as long matches in a 1D stream. That means     
 transposing the strip so columns are stored together, which works as long as glyphs within the same line share vertical alignment.                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm considering a cheaper alternative to explicit glyph sprites: lay out palette-indexed text-line strips column by column, so each glyph becomes a contiguous run of bytes that zstd with a long window can match. I'd compare   
 row-major, column-major per text line, and explicit connected-component sprites to see which gives the best gain.                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm deciding how to handle palette coding for text regions: a per-region palette built from the accessibility node or dirty rect, where anti-aliased text only produces a small ramp of blend levels that can be indexed by

 I'm settling on a page identity for caching: the parent page key combined with the tapped item's stable key, built from the accessibility node's text and resource-id at the tap position. That lets a tap on a row like "WLAN"

 I'm working out how the device would sync the page: B would only store hashes, A keeps the pixels, and I'm considering a per-region summary so B can tell which parts A already has and send only the differences.                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how to keep the page index small: B stores per-page segment hashes (one 8-byte hash per 16 rows) and compares the captured frame against them, sending only a page reference when rows match. For eviction, A

 I'm working out how to keep the cache robust: if A can't resolve a reference, it replies with a miss and B resends the literal, so B's beliefs about A's cache can be wrong without breaking anything. I'm also checking how much

 I'm settling on persisting the encoded tile stream per page in OPFS rather than decoded pixels, since the wire format can double as the storage format, with decoding only when a page is loaded.                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on a content-addressed chunk store for persisted tiles: each chunk is keyed by its hash, and the tile map points to chunk IDs plus row offsets. That way eviction doesn't depend on whether a COPY source page is

 I'm working out how to invalidate overlays: a changed rectangle stays provisional, and if its rows revert to the committed base hash within a TTL the overlay is simply dropped at no byte cost. If the change persists past a

 I'm settling on how ripple and press feedback should be handled in the overlay path, since those short animations would otherwise send many expensive lossless frames that aren't kept anyway. I'm leaning toward lossy encoding

 I'm reworking the frame model around the page map: B captures each frame and maps its scroll region into content coordinates, then sends only tiles that differ from its shadow of A's map. Since A scrolls locally, the viewport 
 offset no longer needs to travel as bytes, and a copy can reference any region already in the map.                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now thinking about the tall virtual display approach: B captures a window about three times the screen height, centered ahead of the scroll direction, so that a local scroll in A can land on content already in the map     
 with no bytes sent. The lead distance scales with scroll velocity and the P95 latency plus a margin. I'm flagging a problem with this: changing the display height changes the app's layout, since bottom bars pinned to the

 I'm weighing whether a tall virtual display fixed for the whole app session would avoid the config-change risk of resizing per page, and how taps would map from A's screen into B's captured window.                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing whether a single always-tall display could handle every page, with the top and bottom bars pinned as fixed slices, instead of resizing the display for each page.                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing the option of resizing the virtual display per qualifying page, which would trigger a config change, so I need to measure the cost of recreation or flicker in M0.                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing a two-phase approach for pages that qualify for tall mode: open at normal height, classify the skeleton, and store a tall_ok flag rather than resizing immediately. I'm also considering an idle-time prefetch where

 I'm weighing the excursion approach against the tall display: with excursions, a tap means B must scroll back into view first, adding about 15–70 ms, while lazy loading and exposure side effects are the same either way.

I'm also estimating the capture cost: a 3× tall window is roughly 31 MB per frame, and hashing that should be about 6–7 ms, which is workable.                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Checking the tall-display size limits: 3× a 2400px-high viewport gives 7200px, which should fit under common GL texture caps, but 4× could exceed 8192 on some GPUs. So the height cap should depend on the device's actual max

 I'm treating the default as a static interface, so scrolling back over cached content or navigating back shouldn't trigger a re-send. Live revalidation would be a per-app or per-page setting. Since the tall display's capture  
 head already covers the visible viewport, that area gets verified without extra cost.

 I'm settling the back-navigation behavior: A shows the cached previous page right away, while B performs the actual Back. B then confirms the resulting page, and if the app handled the back press differently (closing a dialog

 I'm weighing how to choose the tile granularity for diffing: row hashes would help with alignment, while a 2D grid of cell hashes would catch what changed. B can't diff against old pixels since it doesn't keep them, so the

 I'm thinking through how B would diff against cached pages: since B keeps only hashes and not pixels, changed cells get sent as fresh literals, though within a session B could use its in-memory previous frame as a residual

 I'm checking how the image-class pixels behave: they're lossy on A's side, so they can't serve as a shared dictionary or residual reference, and I'd mask them to zeros on both ends. I'm also weighing transport: at roughly

 I'm checking the QUIC datagram size against Tailscale's 1280-byte MTU: about 1252 bytes of UDP payload over IPv4 and 1232 over IPv6, with QUIC's 1200-byte minimum fitting either way. Path MTU probes above that limit would be

 I'm settling the datagram budget now: Tailscale's 1280-byte MTU leaves room for roughly 1150–1170 bytes of QUIC datagram payload after headers, so I'd fix a DGRAM_MAX of 1100 as a protocol constant. Since the default path MTU 
 upper bound of 1452 would just cause dropped probes, I'm leaning toward capping it to match the tunnel. Input and viewport position are the natural fit for datagrams, since viewport state is latest-wins.                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm deciding whether the datagram channel is worth adding now: input is tiny and absolute viewport state is latest-wins, so loss-tolerant datagrams could avoid blocking, but DERP relays over TCP anyway. I'll keep discrete

 I'm looking at how B would order its outgoing streams. The browser's sendOrder only governs A→B streams, so B→A priority has to be set on the server with wtransport's set_priority, and GOAL.md's wording gets that wrong.       
 Priority also only reorders data that hasn't left the send buffer yet, which matters on a 300–800 KB/s link.

 I'm seeing that the pixel-based voting over a global row-hash index can handle scroll displacement, back navigation, re-entry at a different offset, and repeated content with one primitive, with the accessibility skeleton

 I'm sizing the page-index memory next: roughly 200 pages with about 5,000 informative rows each comes to around 16 MB of hashes on B, which is fine to keep persistently. Dropping low-information rows should roughly halve

 I'm weighing whether an overlay should be sent first and only committed to the map once the change has held steady past a stability threshold, so that transient press feedback that reverts never pollutes the cache.            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on explicit Commit and Drop messages for overlays instead of a TTL, so that a brief press effect that reverts costs only a few bytes and never touches the base page cache. For toggles that flip back and forth,

 I'm working through the dim effect now. Computing the backdrop on A with an approximate blend won't match B's capture bit for bit, so I'd rather treat a dialog scrim as a transient overlay that gets dropped when the dialog

 I'm checking whether a dim overlay can be reproduced exactly, so I'd fit the per-channel scale and offset from the (previous, current) pixel pairs and treat any small leftover mismatches as sparse corrections. The alternative 
 is to classify dialog scrims as lossy transient layers, since SurfaceFlinger's 8-bit sRGB blending may not match a simple formula bit for bit.                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm considering whether a dim backdrop should count as a transient overlay rather than a map layer, since it's a transient effect that's fine at ±1 even though IDEA asks for exact pixels elsewhere. I'm leaning toward treating 
 Dim as overlay-only, never committed to the map, with B verifying and sending a ±1 residual only if the dim holds past a threshold. I'm also noting that tall-display dialogs centered in the screen fall outside the single-page

 I'm classifying each floating window by where it sits: top-chrome-overlapping ones stay fixed, bottom-flush ones re-anchor to the viewport bottom, centered ones recenter, and the rest move with the content offset.             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the IME side now: the virtual display could pop up a keyboard on the wrong screen, so I'd set the display IME policy to hide and inject text from A's keyboard instead, which removes that window from the picture.  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking how the bottom bar behaves in the tall display: it sits at the bottom of the tall screen, so it gets pasted back at the viewport's bottom edge. The trickier cases are bars that hide on scroll and toolbars that

 I'm thinking about how a collapsing app bar complicates the scroll model: its state depends on the scroll offset, so at A's offset the toolbar might not look the way it would on B. One fix is to treat the collapsible part as

 I'm checking how the collapsing toolbar and Settings-style headers would behave when the scroll offset is decoupled, since their state depends on scroll position. Rather than modeling sticky headers in full, I'm planning to

 I'm checking how chrome that changes with scroll, like a lift-on-scroll app bar, would be handled, and the plan is to key chrome variants by whether the content is at the top or already scrolled.                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on a scroll mode for each page region: decoupled where the map stays exact and the chrome is invariant or only two-state, so A composites locally and prefetches, and follow mode where the map is inexact, the      
 chrome is coupled to scroll, or nested scrolling is involved, so A waits on B's frames and uses row-shift copy coding.                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm going back to the scroll-offset question: non-uniform item heights make the RecyclerView offset an estimate, so the accessibility-reported offset and range aren't exact. The pixel map itself stays exact, because it's      
 built from rigid displacement of content seen in sequence, and only jumps break that.                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on anchored map segments instead of a single global content offset: uniform item heights let segments be placed absolutely, while non-uniform ones keep local coordinates and get stitched together when overlapping 
 rows match, so gaps from jumps stay explicit.                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm seeing that the segment merge should also cover insertions: when rows after an insertion point match by hash at a shifted offset, the map can split the segment and apply a Splice operation that moves the remainder without 
 sending any pixels. That makes expand and collapse cost nothing for the shifted part, and it generalizes GOAL's block Shift from screen space to content space.                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling the coordinate model as pages made of fixed chrome regions and scroll regions, where each scroll region holds an ordered list of content segments with known or unknown gaps between them. If the viewport crosses

 I'm checking whether the scrollbar can be kept out of the captured pixels, since the app's scrollbar fades in during scrolling and out about a second later. Per-view visibility isn't reachable from outside the app, and the

 I'm settling on how to pick out the scrollbar column: the thumb fades in during scrolling, so for each content row I'd take the first capture where the thumb doesn't cover it, and fill the column from the adjacent background

 I'm settling on a scrollbar approach that keeps the thumb out of the tile hashes: the hash covers only the columns left of the scrollbar strip, and the strip is filled with background-extended pixels while the thumb is        
 visible. A will draw its own scrollbar from the region's content height and viewport, and once the thumb fades I'll run a cleanup pass to patch any strip pixels that turn out to be real content.                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm looking at residual coding now: the idea is a palette mode for text-heavy tiles, since anti-aliased text uses only a few dozen gray levels, so an index map with context modeling should compress far better than zstd on raw

 I'm now weighing how to classify each cell from basic signal statistics: the number of distinct colors (up to a cap), the mean horizontal run length, and the histogram of horizontal gradients. Text should look bimodal, with

 I'm settling on how to tell text from photo-like content in each cell: the fraction of pixels with small nonzero gradients, checked against the color count and A11y hints like ImageView bounds, with the class stored per cell

 I'm working through how to handle the corner pixels of rounded icons, where image and background blend into each other. One option is to code the whole rectangle lossily and fill the area outside the rounded shape with

 I'm considering the corner pixels of image-class rectangles next. Rather than coding corner anti-aliasing losslessly, which costs about as much as the thumbnail itself, I'm leaning toward letting the whole image rectangle go
