 I'm now weighing JPEG against WebP lossy for the image rectangles. WebP comes out roughly 25–35% smaller at equal quality but encodes much more slowly, so I'm starting with JPEG through libjpeg-turbo, since IDEA.md names JPEG

 I'm now weighing a 2D-aware entropy step for the palette index maps: zstd with a long window can pick up repeats at a distance of one row (the stride) as well as far-apart repeated glyphs, which may beat a row-difference

 I'm weighing whether a palette index map with one byte per pixel lets zstd's LZ matching pick up repeated glyphs as short strings at arbitrary offsets, which could get close to WebP lossless at zstd speed, perhaps with a

 I'm now weighing a streaming zstd context per page region, with a large window, so that earlier palette-index data serves as the dictionary on both sides, since the sender has the pixels and the receiver only keeps a RAM

 I'm now thinking about how to store the tile data persistently: a single long-lived zstd context per stream with a large window, so repeated glyph rows and icons are caught at the byte level across frames, and the decoder

 I'm settling on a global, page-level palette with stable index assignment, so identical glyph pixels always map to identical index bytes across tiles. That lets the long-window zstd context find repeated glyph rows across

 I'm now considering how to encode the palette-escape pixels and the fallback tile types: solid, a page-wide palette, local palette, filtered true-color with zstd, and lossy. When the page needs more than 256 colors, I'm

 I'm settling on a global palette of up to 65535 entries, with indices assigned by first appearance so frequent colors get low values. The corpus shows about 700 colors per frame, which is more than 256, so an 8-bit palette

 I'm weighing how to keep palette indices stable across tiles so the long-window zstd context can still match repeated glyphs, since per-cell local palettes break that. One option is to sort each cell's palette by color value,

 I'm weighing the channel-decorrelation idea next: plain RGB-to-green-plus-differences, without the row-difference filter that hurt the earlier text test. Rather than committing to one palette design, I'm leaning toward

 I'm settling on treating the dim as a predictor: fitting a linear a·prev + b per channel over the page, then sending the residual so that any ±1 rounding differences are corrected exactly. Since the default screen is static,

 I'm now looking at how to detect motion and classify regions with cheap signal features. Beyond exact row-hash matching, I'm considering 1D projection profiles and normalized cross-correlation so that non-exact, sub-pixel or  
 oversampled scrolling can still be recognized.                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighting each row by how rare its hash is in the frame, so periodic rows like list separators stop producing false matches, instead of just counting color transitions.                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm weighing the voting step for motion detection: a histogram of vertical offsets over matched row pairs, where a peak only counts if it clearly beats the second peak, since a bare vote threshold is too loose. Periodic lists 
 with identical item rows would produce comb-like peaks at multiples of the item pitch, so I'm planning to break that tie using the offset B itself injected, which is known in advance.                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Since B injects the scroll itself, the expected dy is known in advance, so I can verify the match in a small window around that offset instead of estimating motion blindly. That is cheaper and also breaks ties in periodic     
 lists. Blind voting only remains for motion the app starts on its own, like smooth-scroll animations or keyboard panning. I'm also considering autocorrelation of row signatures, or the A11y child bounds, to find the item      
 pitch.                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm settling on content-defined tile boundaries: when A11y bounds are available, cut tiles at item edges so identical list items dedupe by hash even after a shift, and without them, cut at runs of blank separator rows.        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working through the layer classification step: sorting each block by how many distinct colors it has and how its gradient histogram looks, so that flat UI and text separate from photographic content.                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm sorting blocks into classes: flat or palette-like content, text and graphics with few colors and a bimodal gradient profile, and photographic regions with many colors and lots of small gradients.                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm moving on to how to pick out individual sprites, by finding connected blobs in the non-background mask and keying them by shape and color hash, sized roughly 8 to 256 pixels.                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether glyph sprites can be deduplicated at all, since text subpixel positioning could make the same glyph render as different bitmaps depending on its x-offset. On Android, TextView usually renders at integer   
 pixel positions, so identical glyphs should produce identical bitmaps, but Compose may differ.                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking whether glyph deduplication pays off at all, since subpixel text positioning could make identical glyphs render differently, and CJK text has far more distinct characters than Latin. The only real evidence so far 
 is the −8.4% offline number, so I'd rather run a quick corpus experiment at M5 than build it blind. Node-level sprites keyed by the A11y node rectangle might catch repeated labels and icons more cheaply.                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working through dim detection next: fitting the per-channel relation between the previous and current pixels, though a scrim's rounding may not reproduce exactly across GPUs.                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out the residual for the dim overlay: if the rounding is a fixed per-channel function of the previous pixel value, the correction could be a lookup table rather than a random-noise patch, which would keep it far   
 smaller than a full-screen residual.                                                                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working through how to detect a uniform dim overlay: if each previous pixel value always maps to the same current value within a region, that mapping can be stored as a small per-channel lookup table rather than a full

 I'm settling on a Remap overlay for the dim layer: a per-channel lookup table over the previous pixel values, which stays exact where a fixed alpha rounding wouldn't. The dimming then has to be applied at view time rather

 I'm working out how the spinner case fits the same pattern: a small rect that changes every frame with a fixed period should repeat its content hashes, so once one cycle has been seen, each frame can be a reference into the

 I'm settling on a spinner approach that sends the loop once as a sprite sequence, so the device animates it locally and needs no per-frame updates while it spins. I'm also checking whether forcing animator duration scale to

 I'm noting that the spinner would only move if animator duration scale stays above zero, so it's low priority, and I'd cap small periodic regions at about 10 fps by dropping frames in the Overlay class. Since Overlay updates

 I'm working out the capture cost for the taller display: at 3× height each frame is around 34 MB, so hashing would take roughly 8 ms with SIMD, which is workable at about 30 fps. Since A composes the scroll locally, B doesn't 
 need smooth scroll animation and can instead move its capture window in discrete jumps.                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm estimating the cost per second of scrolling with discrete jumps: each jump produces a frame where only the newly revealed rows are fresh content. The real limit here is bandwidth rather than CPU, since a text list screen  
 is roughly 70–150KB, which puts sustainable scrolling at a few screens per second at best.                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working out how far scrolling can get before bandwidth runs out: the prefetch lead depends on latency, but if scroll speed times bytes per pixel exceeds the link rate, no lead helps and blank blocks appear. So I'm         
 considering a degradation ladder, starting with a low-fidelity placeholder such as a half-resolution or blurred preview that gets sharpened later, and computing the maximum sustainable scroll speed from the link rate.         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the throughput side: at around 3 screens/s and 0.3 s of latency, the lead works out to about one screen, which fits a 3–4× tall display. Next I want to see whether IDEA's prefetch formula, lead = scroll speed ×   
 (P95 draw time + margin), accounts for link bandwidth at all.                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm noting that as lead grows, queueing delay grows too, so the prefetch needs to be treated as a rate-control problem: keep a buffer of content ahead in the scroll direction, target a lead of scroll speed times P95 latency,

 Looking at the budget now: first-seen full-screen pages run from about 64 KB to 2.3 MB, so at 300–800 KB/s a lossless photo-like frame costs several seconds, while a typical tap transition is closer to a fraction of a second. 
 That makes first-seen pages and page changes, not scrolling, the main latency target, so the plan should prioritize caching rendered pages and coding flat UI regions efficiently.

 Now I'm sorting out which layer the "图片图层" in the IDEA means, since the notes list bg, lit, and fg as three separately tunable layers.                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm mapping the three layers onto the image/text/video classes: text and flat UI go to the lossless background layer, images and icons go to the lossy sprite-pool layer, and video regions go to the foreground layer.       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm now sorting out the IDEA's wording, which conflicts with GOAL on what fg covers: the IDEA lists fg as the video region, while GOAL also treats images as fg. I'm settling on the IDEA mapping, where the image class goes to  
 the sprite-pool layer and fg stays reserved for video.                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the displacement detection ideas: row-hash voting limited to the scroll region minus the scrollbar columns, weighted by how much information each row carries.                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working through how to speed up the displacement check: since the scroll amount is known in advance, I can first verify the expected offset directly, falling back to a full vote only on mismatch.                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm thinking about how to speed up the row voting: I'd weight each row's match by how rare its hash is in the previous region, so repeated rows like list separators count for less, and split the columns into a few bands   
 so a change in one column doesn't throw off the others. Sticky and collapsing headers would still need repeated displacement rounds, and I'd run the same voting on columns for horizontal scrolling.                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at how to make displacement detection faster and more robust, like using the commanded scroll delta as a prior and weighting repeated rows less so list separators don't cause false peaks.                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm describing the overlay as a second plane on each end, separate from the persistent base tile map. Non-scroll changes land there first and only get promoted to base once they stay stable past a commit threshold with no 
 touch down, while a return to the base hash clears them.                                                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm treating the tint case as one mechanism: a per-rect affine prediction from the base pixels, which covers the pressed highlight, the dim backdrop, and disabled greying, with only a small residual left over to encode.   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling how to keep the scrollbar out of the base tiles: its columns fade about 550 ms after scrolling stops, so tiles captured mid-scroll get those columns marked dirty and refreshed once the thumb is gone.          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling how the scrollbar stays out of the base tiles: its columns fade roughly 550 ms after scrolling stops, so I'd exclude those right-edge columns from hashing and only commit their pixels from frames where the    
 thumb is gone.                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing how to send the server-side priority for the three streams: WebTransport's sendOrder only governs what A sends, so for B's outgoing data I'd set the stream priority on the Rust side, where buffered            
 higher-priority data goes out first, in line with the GOAL's reliable-stream scheme.                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm correcting the GOAL's claim that sendOrder handles visible-region priority: that API only governs what the browser sends, so the downlink priority has to be set on the Rust side. To make preemption real, I'm keeping   
 the prefetch stream's in-flight buffer small and giving each prefetch batch its own stream so a stale one can be reset.                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how the transport limits the lead: a visible-patch stream is fine as a single ordered stream, and the bandwidth estimate should come from acked bytes over time rather than one fixed P95, since tile size    
 changes the drawing delay. Solving that relation for the lead distance suggests a hard limit: once scroll speed times bytes per pixel approaches the link rate, the lead blows up and can't be covered.                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the throughput ceiling: at 300 KB/s, roughly 60 bytes per row for a text list gives a maximum scroll speed near 5000 px/s, about two screens per second, while icon-heavy lists drop below one screen per        
 second.                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm working through the frontier problem: with no fling, scroll speed is capped by the user's own drag, and I'd clamp or soften the scroll at the prefetched edge. I also want a two-pass prefetch, sending the cheap text layer  
 first so the frontier advances on roughly 20–40 bytes per row, which is an estimate from the corpus PNG sizes.                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the datagram size budget: over Tailscale's 1280-byte MTU, subtracting the IPv6 and UDP headers leaves about 1232 bytes of UDP payload, and QUIC framing, the AEAD tag, and the WebTransport session ID eat a few 
 dozen more.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out the datagram size budget: Tailscale's MTU leaves roughly 1200 bytes of UDP payload after headers, so I'd pin the MTU discovery upper bound and size datagram messages around 1100 bytes, checking             
 max_datagram_size() at runtime rather than hardcoding it.                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at the datagram question: Tailscale's MTU leaves a UDP payload of about 1232 bytes, and I'm considering which messages, like pointer and scroll-position samples, could go as loss-tolerant datagrams while pixel 
 data stays on reliable streams.                                                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm noting that the datagram size should stay conservative for v1, matching the earlier decision to measure before turning datagrams on, and I'm checking the Tailscale MTU setup in quinn: initial MTU 1200, upper bound     
 pinned to 1232, with the default black-hole cooldown and discovery interval. The certificate side is next: the serverCertificateHashes approach needs ECDSA P-256 with validity under two weeks, so B has to regenerate its       
 certificate on start once the remaining validity gets short.                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at the certificate hash that goes into the URL: it rotates whenever the certificate is regenerated, so the launcher URL changes with it, and I'm weighing whether to print the new URL from B on start instead of 
 trying to keep the hash stable.                                                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling how the WebUI gets served on localhost, weighing a small static server on A against adb forward.                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out the input model: A's viewport is decoupled from B's real scroll position, so taps get sent in content coordinates and B has to scroll to the spot before injecting the touch.                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out the input model: taps get the hash of the tile row under the finger, so B can reject a stale target and send a fault back instead. Because speculative cached content could be wrong, taps on anything A      
 hasn't yet confirmed from B have to wait until B verifies that tile.                                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out the back-stack tracking: instead of polling dumpsys every 50–80 ms, B can listen for UiAutomation window-state events and use skeleton hash changes to detect fragment transitions, keeping a stack of page   
 IDs that pushes a new page after a tap lands on a different one.                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the back-stack design: A keeps a stack of page states, pushing when a tap lands on a new page and popping when Back returns to the previous one, and I'm weighing whether the shell can listen for task-stack    
 changes or whether accessibility window events plus skeleton hashes are enough, with dumpsys as a fallback.                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at how to store the cache in OPFS, which only allows synchronous access inside a Worker, so the decoder and cache would run there. Compressed tile blobs go in content-addressed storage with per-page indexes    
 and an LRU manifest, deduplicated across pages by hash, and I'd ask for persistent storage to reduce eviction.                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling how the cache is keyed: the namespace comes from the device, display size and density, font scale, dark mode, locale and app version, so a dark-mode toggle doesn't wipe the light cache. If B loses its         
 per-page index after a reboot, I'd have A send its page summaries at hello so B can rebuild it.                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm deciding that A stays the source of truth for cache contents while B holds no state across restarts. A would send its segment hashes for a page when B enters it, and B could verify them against live strip hashes       
 without needing the pixels.                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm thinking about where the hash lists should live: B could keep a persisted copy as a cache of A's summary, checking it against A's page root and asking for the full summary only when the roots differ. I'm also weighing 
 whether 64-bit row hashes are safe enough for verifying tile identity across restarts.                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm thinking about how to make the hash for tile IDs safe across stores: 128-bit for tile identity, 64-bit row hashes over the masked columns, plus a periodic full-viewport verification check on A's side in debug mode.    
 Next is how fixed elements like a floating button or bottom nav sitting over the scroll region break the row-shift matching.                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how fixed elements like a floating button or bottom nav break row matching: their rows don't shift with the scroll, so I'd detect them as pixels that stay put while the content moves, accumulating a        
 per-page pinned mask, and use accessibility nodes that overlap the scroll rect but aren't its children as a prior.                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling how fixed elements over the scroll region get handled: a FAB or translucent bottom bar would be composited as a fixed layer above the tiles, with anything it hides marked unknown until it scrolls out from     
 under it. Translucent overlays can't be cleanly separated, so those would either stream from B after the scroll settles or keep the page out of tall mode. I also still need to work out how tall-display virtual displays get    
 created from the shell via reflection.                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling the tall virtual display setup: creating it from the shell via reflection the way scrcpy does, with the flags for owning its content, touch support, trust, and no touch feedback, plus the newer-API flags      
 where available, and system decorations off so there's no status or nav bar. For text input, I'm weighing the IME policy options.                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling the height cap for the tall display, deriving it from the GL texture limit rather than taking the 3–4x figure from the goal as given.                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling the height cap for the tall display, with the probing done at startup: try a few multiples of the screen height and keep the largest one the app handles without crashing, cached per device. Frame copying is   
 the real cost, since a 1080×9600 RGBA frame is about 41MB and would need a mitigation beyond what ImageReader gives me.                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how tap coordinates map onto the tall display, which should be a direct content-to-y mapping without a pre-scroll step.                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm thinking about the tall virtual display as a live window k screens high, so A can scroll within it instantly with content verified live rather than guessed ahead. Once the viewport nears an edge of that window, the    
 tall screen itself scrolls to recentre, and the bottom bar sits at the bottom of the tall screen.                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how the bottom of the tall window is detected: a scrollable node that no longer offers the forward-scroll action is at the end, so prefetch can stop there. For paginated feeds, the tall display may trigger    
 more loading, so I'd bound how far ahead it prefetches.                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at the global settings: setting the window and transition animation scales to zero, and weighing whether the animator duration scale can be adjusted without breaking some apps' ripples and spinners. I'm also   
 considering disabling window blurs through the global settings key, though MIUI may have its own blur toggles.                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm thinking about the watchdog for restoring the animation settings: a small shell loop that watches the daemon's PID and restores the originals when it dies, since a hard kill can't run any handlers. I'm also making     
 sure the process survives an adb disconnect, and noting that MIUI's power manager may send SIGTERM that needs handling.                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm noting that the daemon's UiAutomation registration would clash with Appium's UiAutomator2 server, since only one UiAutomation can be registered system-wide, so the recorder and the daemon can't run on the same device  
 at once.                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing whether to drop Appium entirely, since it can't capture the virtual display from another process, and instead build the recorder into our own Kotlin host so it uses the same capture, accessibility, and input  
 path as production.                                                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking whether Appium's UiAutomator2 server would clash with the daemon: it registers its own UiAutomation, and only one can be registered system-wide, so the two can't run on the same device at once. That points    
 toward building the recorder into our own Kotlin host, using the same capture, accessibility and input path as production.                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm planning the evaluation harness, separating a recorded capture from the offline benchmark so that different encoder versions can be compared on the same input. The closed-loop pieces like prefetch, head moves and the  
 tall display still need to be checked against that capture.                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm sketching the offline evaluation side: a simulator that replays recorded pages as long images, answers what the display would show at any head position, and pushes the frames through the encoder and a modeled link     
 with bandwidth, latency and jitter, so the A-side viewport can be measured without depending on a live device.                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm sketching a second tier of the corpus: a world simulator built from recorded page content rather than flat frames, so prefetch and head-position heuristics can be tuned offline. Frames from real sessions would still   
 be needed to tune classification and overlay rules against scrcpy, but the scroll-driven behavior needs the simulated pages.                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing how to compare against scrcpy fairly: at matched bitrate caps, the question is how many pixels survive exactly and how quickly the content shows up.                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm planning the milestones, splitting M0 so the recorder, the offline bench, and the scrcpy baseline come first as their own step.                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing the M0 feasibility spikes: checking tall-display resize per app, wheel exactness per container type, ScrollToPosition, A11y on the virtual display, and WebTransport with MTU over Tailscale, each with its own  
 pass/fail check that decides which branch to take. I'm also thinking about tying acceptance criteria to the link budget, and whether the page cache should come before or alongside scrolling given that prefetch is the main UX  
 priority.                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling the ordering: build one content-addressed tile store first, since scroll-back, page return and sprite reuse can all run off the same map, then layer scroll detection and prefetch on top.                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm reworking the operation set into two planes: a single content-addressed store for definitions, base-plane placements, and transient overlay ops with a commit/clear step.                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling the operation set for the plan: a content-addressed store holds every definition, and placements point at stored tile ids, so copies cost no pixel bytes. Transient overlays stay on a separate plane with a     
 commit or clear step, and I'm keeping the wire format as a brief skeleton rather than a detailed spec.                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how to pack the palette: each tile gets its own palette of up to 256 colors, or a 10-bit index when a whole page has more than that, since the settings frames use around 580 to 750 distinct colors. I'm     
 also weighing how to order the palette so the anti-aliasing ramps sit next to each other in index space.                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing a zstd-based approach on the palette index planes, using the previous tiles on the same page as a dictionary, against building glyph sprites from connected-component hashes. The earlier ablation showed        
 sprites saving only about 8% offline, but hashing connected components needs no font sync, so I want to measure both on the same index data before choosing.                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking how often the per-frame color counts stay under 256, 1024, 4096, or above 20000, since that share decides whether a background palette is worth building first.                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm planning the client side: the viewer will draw from GPU textures for the visible region plus a lookahead margin, decode tiles in a Worker so scrolling never stalls, and keep compressed data in OPFS with an LRU atlas   
 in memory.                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at how accessibility data gets fetched: pulling the full tree is slow on large screens, so I'd rather refresh it only on content-change events and cache the scrollable node, treating the accessibility info as  
 hints while the pixels stay the source of truth.                                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing how accessibility fetches should be configured: flagging the service to report view IDs and include not-important views so the skeleton stays stable, and considering prefetch-descendant flags on newer API     
 levels to cut down on IPC round trips.                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing whether page-change detection should wait for the accessibility skeleton, which takes 50–200 ms to arrive. Sending the background immediately into a provisional page avoids that delay, but may waste bytes on  
 pages that are already cached, so I'm considering checking content hashes against tiles from likely neighboring pages first.                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm weighing whether to predict the next page from navigation edges recorded per tap target, so A could show a cached page optimistically at tap time while B verifies it. The risk is a mis-tap or a visual flash when the   
 prediction is wrong, so I'm leaning toward making optimistic forward navigation opt-in per app.                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out how to index the pages for lookup: a full per-row hash table would be too large, so I'm considering one anchor hash per small segment of rows instead, which would let a new frame vote for its likely page   
 by content.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm looking at how to relocate a returning scroll position: instead of indexing every row, I'd keep only content-defined anchors (rows whose hash hits a fixed residue), so the index shrinks by about 32x and a first-screen 
 hash can still find its place on the page map regardless of alignment. Winnowing fits here because it guarantees a minimum density of anchors.                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the A11y side on the virtual display: I'd read all windows per display through the windows-on-all-displays call, which needs the retrieve-interactive-windows flag, rather than relying on the active window of  
 the default display.                                                                                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm adding a point about per-frame processing cost: the encoder runs in Rust through a direct buffer, and since damage regions are unknown, I'd hash every row each frame, which the old numbers suggest is cheap enough. I   
 also need to check that the app whitelist is enforced on the device side, since the open command carries a token in the URL, and that the launch targets the virtual display through the activity-options route.                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 I'm checking the foreign-package cases in the dumps, where 49 of 451 show a different root package, such as settings opening the intelligence service, OTA, or the launcher. Since a whitelist by package would also block        
 legitimate Settings sub-pages, I'm leaning toward allowing activities started within the session's task instead.                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the device's side-by-side margins: the root bounds sit at 53 px on each side, though I'm not sure whether that comes from a large-screen layout or an edge-to-edge inset, and it doesn't change the plan. The    
 remaining question is the size of the virtual display relative to the 1080 px capture width that feeds the canvas.                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm settling on a fixed virtual display profile, say 1080 px wide at 420 dpi, so the cache key stays stable across window resizes. A's viewport height can differ from B's display height, since the map is composed on A, so 
 I only need to pin width and density and scale in CSS.                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm going through the list of gaps in the spec: the layer assignment for foreground content conflicts between sections, the downlink priority is on the wrong side, tile addressing only handles vertical offsets, and        
 there's no baseline or deterministic trace recorder yet. I also need to check the differential-update rule and the drag injection for the head.                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm going through the remaining spec gaps: the WebUI items like the left and right keys, per-layer quality, history and clipboard, and the whitelist picker aren't fully covered, and the M-order puts page caching at M3     
 after scrolling at M2.                                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm deciding the format for the deliverable: I'll rewrite GOAL.md in Chinese with terse structure and marked evidence, then report the changes, key findings, and assumptions in chat, noting I skipped tests and didn't read 
 the cmp-scp or corpus code.                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm deciding how to write GOAL.md: a thorough but navigable Chinese design doc of roughly 250–330 lines, with each claim tagged by its evidence level, such as source-verified, corpus-measured, or carried over from the old 
 tests.                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm checking the color distribution in the metadata to see whether the palette approach holds, and whether the Xiaomi settings skeleton hashes collide across sub-pages with different titles, since the page key will need   
 extra discriminators.                                                                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm working out the MTU budget: Tailscale's interface MTU is 1280, so the inner UDP payload is about 1252 bytes over IPv4 and 1232 over IPv6. I'd clamp the path MTU discovery upper bound to 1232 to be safe for both, which 
 still clears QUIC's 1200-byte minimum. Then the usable datagram size is that MTU minus the QUIC header overhead, and I still need to confirm how quinn's default connection ID length affects it.                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 Now I'm estimating the usable datagram payload after QUIC overhead, landing around 1.1 KB, so the design limit of 1024 bytes should hold. Next I'll run the quick checks on the color distribution, the Xiaomi settings skeleton

 I'm now on how scroll displacement gets estimated: row hashes voted like a sparse cross-correlation between the previous and current frames. The weak spot is that identical rows, like separators or periodic list patterns, can

 Now I'm looking at how the scroll check should work against the accessibility events. The throttle batches scroll deltas into roughly 100ms windows and only reports them accumulated, so they lag the frames. That means I can

 I'm checking how each scrollable container reports its position: RecyclerView and ListView only expose a delta plus the adapter index of the visible items, while ScrollView and WebView also give an absolute offset and maximum 
 range, which makes them easier to calibrate against.                                                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
 For recyclers and list views, the accessibility tree reports each visible item's adapter position, so I could key the tile map by item index and the row within that item instead of raw pixel offsets. That would give an

 I'm working out how RecyclerView and ListView can expose item indices through the accessibility tree, so the tile map could be keyed by item position rather than raw pixel offsets. I'm also checking how ScrollTo-position
